speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S POSITION WITH RESPECT TO PACIFIC SETTLEMENT OF INTERNATIONAL DISPUTES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I notice in this morning's press that Great Britain and France have informed the League of Nations that they will not consider binding their obligations under the general act for pacific settlement of international disputes in the event that either country should be at war. I should like to know whether Canada, as an independent signatory to that agreement, also repudiates the idea of arbitration instead of war.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S POSITION WITH RESPECT TO PACIFIC SETTLEMENT OF INTERNATIONAL DISPUTES
speechtext: I do not know that I would care to answer the question in just the form in which my hon. friend has stated it, but I would say to him that Canada has not altered her position.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, February 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King that the house go into committee on the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the trade agreement entered into
at Washington on the 17th day of November, 1938. between Canada and the United States of America, and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to-day in a sense I am replying to the speech made by my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) three days ago. I must say that at least half of his speech did not deal with the trade treaty at all but was good political propaganda, from his standpoint. My hon. friend from Mount Royal, whose observations are very wise and very apt, remarked to me that if the text of the trade treaty had smallpox certainly the sermon the right hon. gentleman delivered would escape contagion because it was so far from the text. I thought that was rather well put. I do not intend to follow my right hon. friend into the political realm-I was going to say "quagmire" but will not use that word-except for two or three remarks.
My right hon. friend spoke of the byelections and boasted a little-perhaps with some justification-in regard to the number of seats his party had won. I happen to have the correct figures, which show that in the fourteen contested by-elections since 1935 the Liberal vote was 111,000, while the antiLiberal vote was 131,000, so there is not very much to boast about there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: But those were not all Conservative votes.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That is true, but they were in opposition to the Liberals. In the 1935 general election, only 46 per cent of the votes went Liberal while 54 per cent went antiLiberal. In spite of that fact, however, my hon. friends obtained 180 seats as against 65 seats won by the 54 per cent voting against the Liberals. Another interesting set of figures -and then I shall have done with the ordinary political discussion-shows that according to the votes cast in the last election it took 12,000 odd votes to elect a Liberal. I do not use the word "odd" in any derogatory sense. It took 33,000 odd votes to elect a Conservative, and it took 389.000 votes to elect the hon. gentleman from Kootenay East. I do not know what any of these figures prove, however; they merely indicate some of the rather strange pictures we get if we begin to describe what we call democracy. The only point I make is that, according to these figures, I do not think my right hon. friend has such a great deal to boast about.
The right hon. gentleman mentioned differences in our party respecting the tariff. Well, perhaps there are such differences, but there

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
are differences in all parties. So far as the tariff is concerned the Liberal party goes from the extreme of free trade, as represented by my hon. friend from Huron North (Mr. Deach-man) and many members from the west, to moderately high protection, at least, as represented by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). So not only in regard to the tariff but in regard to almost everything, you can go up and down in the Liberal party from imperialism to Hepburnism, and you will find differences of opinion. But after all, sir, the trade agreement is the subject before the house, and I intend to deal with it as briefly as possible having regard to the fact that a great deal of ground must be covered.
To me. I think to all of us, the subject is a very important one which merits free discussion. I do not think any party or any government can bring into effect a trade treaty of any kind without its deserving in this House of Commons free and wide discussion. For example, the debate on the empire trade agreements of 1932 took twenty-six parliamentary days. In fact, we began the sixth week; there were nineteen days on the resolution, and seven days in committee. At the end my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his party, who were in opposition at the time, voted against the empire trade agreements-with the exception of the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) who on the second reading voted for it, but I think abstained from voting at the other stages of the measure. In 1911, when the reciprocity agreement was being discussed, the debate took, I believe, something over four months.
In view of those two points it is clear that this subject is too important to gloss over, and requires a certain amount of elucidation. I have pointed out, and I wish to make it clear, that it is not in any way the intention of this party to hold up the discussion. We have no interest in delaying the business of the house or unnecessarily prolonging the debate. In fact I have no doubt the debate will be a good deal shorter-that is my guess at this time-than was the debate on the empire trade agreements. We realize that after all the government has a huge majority, and can pass the legislation anyway.
But I repeat that a fair discussion is proper, both as we sit at the moment and in committee; for it is only right that the details should be discussed. After all, this is public business of the utmost importance to Canada- just as, to my mind, the Bren gun was public business. And I do not mind saying to-day that I am getting just a little tired of people

outside of the house, who know nothing whatever about the affairs of parliament, or how they are carried on, continually lecturing this house and urging it to get on with the business of the people. I do not care who they are; I think they are lecturing without sufficient knowledge. After all, the government of Canada is the executive of parliament, and parliament, therefore-theoretically at least, and indeed in practice-has the last word. That is democracy. Whatever the faults of democracy may be, at any rate it is superior to anything we know of in the way of dictatorship.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I think I am expressing the point of view of every hon. member in the house when I say that those who criticize members of the House of Commons, as a body, simply because we choose to discuss matters here, merely show that they do not quite understand what the democratic liberty of free speech means.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: As a matter of fact-and I do not say this with the intention of playing politics-my conviction is that the reason we did not go on a few days ago when we could have was that the government was not ready.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: No. no.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
And to show I am not trying to play politics, I say that because I well remember that on some occasions hon. gentlemen on this side were in office we were not ready to proceed. For some reason, governments are often not quite ready with the business of the house. I remember occasions when we had to do what my right hon. friend had to do on a few occasions this year-when we had to adjourn the house at six o'clock. Frankly, I do not know why persons who are not members of the house insist that we should work here until eleven o'clock every night. In fact I will admit that one of the very fine things the right hon. gentleman had much to do with, was that of changing the foolish habit we used to have of sitting here late every night-a most barbarous procedure. After all, we have some rights in the way of liberty and freedom, in regard to our hours, as well as in regard to our speech.
My right hon. friend in his political remarks the other day, suggested that this party consists of economic nationalists, that we do not want to trade with other countries. Of course, that, to put it mildly is ridiculous,-only a blind man in a country like Canada would

Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement
take any such course as that. There are two chief reasons why Canada must trade with other countries. In the first place we have a huge area, a small population and rich resources, out of which we produce large quantities of raw materials which must be exported. We do not consume all of them ourselves. That, in the first place, compels us to trade with other countries. Secondly, we are a debtor nation. The other day I looked up the exact figures and I found that each year we pay out in interest on dominion, provincial, municipal and large corporation loans from other countries, in round figures, S250.000.000 per year. Indeed, we pay out $325,000,000, but we receive in return, in the form of interest and dividends, something like $78,000,000, leaving a balance, in round figures, of about $250,000.000 per year, which we have to pay out to other countries. Most of it goes to the United States-$231,000,000-as against $88,000,000 to the United Kingdom.
So that for that reason again we must export. I must point out however that in our export statistics to-day we include gold, and I believe that does not give quite the proper picture. Gold should be kept separate from ordinary commodities, because gold is not a commodity in the ordinary sense. It is something which is accepted by all countries of the world-they are glad to take it-and for that reason it is something which should not be treated as an ordinary commodity in trade statistics.
In addition to all that, there is a third reason why we must trade. There are certain kinds of products which we cannot produce- tea, coffee, rubber, cotton and even, apparently, wool, though we should, to my mind, be able to produce sufficient wool; I have said that in the house many times. We do not produce oranges and other citrus fruits, and so on. So we are compelled to trade.
Then again, trade figures are mixed up with invisible items such as the tourist trade, shipping, insurance, and the interest wrhich I have just mentioned. So I say that the right hon. gentleman's statement that we do not want to trade, and that we do not want trade treaties, is not correct, and he knows it is not correct. Anyone who knows something about government business or national affairs realizes that we must trade with other countries. But what we do favour is this: We favour trading with other countries on a fair basis. We advocate giving favour for favour. In other words, we do not advocate the making of a trade treaty at any price. I am a pacifist in the best sense of the word; I do not believe in war. But I am not a
pacifist at any price; neither am I a trade treaty man, at any price. If we are to take the attitude that we will make a trade treaty at any price-that is, give two favours for one, if necessary, to get a trade treaty-then the logical conclusion for my right hon. friend and his part}' to come to is to become out and out free traders. Then they would be getting all the imports that our exports could pay for, and there would be no tariff barriers against them.
The only countries of the world to-day in which economic nationalism prevails are a few of the European countries which became economically nationalist because of the great war, and the fear of another one. They would wish if another war came upon them to be self-supporting, self-sufficient and able to take care of themselves. Perhaps of all the countries in the world the United States is the closest to being self-supporting or self-sufficient; yet even the United States requires rubber, tea, coffee, and some other products it cannot produce within its own borders.
Now, in regard to the empire trade agreements,' which are mixed up with the one before us, we must not forget that the United Kingdom is the greatest market of the world. That is obvious to anyone who looks at the figures. It is the greatest purchasing market of the world.
I have a quotation in my hand-and I have heard only a part of it cited before-from the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. This is the report of a speech he made m Toronto, in the Toronto Globe of April 2. 1907, at a banquet given to Right Hon. James Bryce, then British ambassador at Washington. This is what Sir Wilfrid said at that time:
I have seen and you have all seen in an American newspaper published in New York just a few days ago, that we are yearning for reciprocity with the United States. Now I tell you that the editor of that neryspaper is about twenty-five years behind the times. At that time, we would have given our right arm for such a thing, but it is now a thing of the past. We are turning our hopes towards the old motherland. We have introduced the doctrine and the policy of a preference to Great Britain and towards all the British empire, and this is the policy by which we stand at the present time. We shall have no more pilgrimages to Washington, and this is simply the message I have to convey to your guest at the present moment. I know he will be a friend of Canada, and if it be a fact that a new leaf be turned in our relations w'ith our neighbours it will be a matter for great congratulation.
The right hon. gentleman who now leads the government of Canada frequently quotes what Sir Wilfrid Laurier had done, and he might give some consideration to the "no more pilgrimages to Washington" idea. I intend to

deal with the fact that we also looked for a trade treaty, but we looked for one on a different basis from the one negotiated by the right hon. gentleman. To go back a little further, it was the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier which in 1897 introduced the British preference. I could not find the exact quotation-hon. members opposite will correct me, I am sure, if I am wrong-but I think I am right when I say that for some years Sir Wilfrid took the attitude that we should get something in return, something by way of preference from Great Britain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Sir Wilfrid's position was that if at any time England became a protectionist country, we should then expect to be given' a preference in the British market.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I attempted to look it up but I could not find it. I accept what the right hon. gentleman has said; and that is exactly what we advocated and what we accomplished in the end. While Great Britain was a free trading country she could hardly give any preference or advantage to the different portions of the empire, but once she became protectionist-I pointed out the other day, Great Britain collects three times as much customs duties per capita as we do- it was then possible for her to return favour for favour, to return something for the favours which she had been receiving since 1897. I submit that the empire trade agreements negotiated in 1932 by the Bennett government were a great triumph.
Great Britain is not only the greatest market in the world, but she is a sheltered market; and that was particularly valuable once we got a preference: the preference gave us shelter. There is another point that should be considered, and that is the fact that Great Britain is a static market; in other words, her population remains practically stationary, and she does not increase her purchases from the world. She goes on buying the same amount of commodities, aside from armaments, year in and year out. It is worth remembering that it is our loss when the United States, competing with us in that market in products such as wheat, fruits and lumber, get some of our export business. If by this treaty we lose in exports to Great Britain, granting world conditions remain the same, ours will not. We would be increasing our unemployment and our distress through allowing the United States to take some of the market which previously we had enjoyed.
As I admitted a moment ago, we also wanted a trade treaty. But in seeking it we asked for it on a fair basis. We did not

attempt to get that trade treaty, or trade agreement-I am using the terms interchangeably-except on a basis of favour for favour. After all, there are many reasons why we should get fair treatment from the United States. I have before me the letters exchanged between the Canadian and United States governments in 1934. The right hon. Prime Minister quoted them the other day. I have no intention of reading all the letters, which were issued as a white paper in 1935. I suggest to any hon. members who have not read this white paper that they do so; they will find it very interesting. The letter from which I intend to quote is dated at Washington, November 14, 1934, and is signed by Hon. W. D. Herridge, who was then our representative at Washington. It is addressed to Mr. Cordell Hull, and reads as follows:
The government of Canada for many months have been giving careful consideration to the means whereby the exchange of commodities between Canada and the United States might be increased, and I have been instructed to present a statement of their views for the information of the government of the United States. The government of Canada believe that the time has come for definite action and that the declared desire of both governments to improve conditions of trade between the two countries should now be carried into effect by the negotiation of a comprehensive trade agreement.
You will recall that when the Prime Minister of Canada visited Washington in April, 1933, at the invitation of the President of the United States, the development of trade between the two countries was sympathetically discussed.
I think the right hon. Prime Minister quoted that the other day. Then lower down in his letter, Mr. Herridge says:
Since Mr. Bennett's visit, informal discussions have been carried on, and several methods of improving trade relations between the two countries have been suggested and examined.
I should like to quote further from the letter, a part which applies particularly to this discussion. It reads:
It is hardly necessary to stress the importance to both the United States and Canada of their mutual trade. For many years each country has provided the other with either its largest or its second largest foreign market.
Here is an interesting part a little further down:
During the decade ending in 1933 Canada provided a market for the products of the United States larger by one-fourth than the whole of Asia, about twice as large as Germany or all South America, nearly three times as large as France or Japan, nearly seven times as large as China, and more than ten times as large as the Soviet Union. In spite of the considerable decline in trade from the high level of 1929, Canada still provided a market in the first nine months of 1934 only slightly smaller than all Asia, nearly twice as large

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
as all South America or Japan, between two and three times as large as Germany or France, four times as large as China, and twenty-two times as large as the Soviet Union.
Then he continues on the next page:
In no year since 1882 have Canadian exports to the United States exceeded in value Canadian imports from the United States.
Since that was written in 1934 there have been a couple of years when Canadian exports to the United States were slightly larger than Canadian imports from the United States, but apparently those are the facts up to that time. The letter continues:
During the thirty years ending in 1933, Canada purchased in the United States almost 70 per cent of all her imports and sold in the United States only 37 per cent of all her exports. In the last decade, Canadians have spent over $1.60 in buying products of the United States for every dollar spent on Canadian products by purchasers in' the United States.
That is not a per capita comparison.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It is a better comparison.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That is a matter of opinion. I am not quite in agreement with the hon. gentleman, but he will have a chance to deal with the matter later on. I am not going to argue about it at the moment. The letter goes on:
Canada has therefore been obliged to meet the debit balance thus arising by other means of payment. In the decade 1921 to 1930, according to the Department of Commerce of the United States, the balance payable by Canada to the United States on exchange of commodities averaged $287 millions a year.
That is a huge balance in favour of the United States. Then on page 8 he said:
Since the beginning of the depression, amongst countries heavily indebted to the United States, Canada stands almost alone in having promptly discharged in full its obligations payable in the United States.
I am pointing this out because I remarked at the beginning of my speech that the United States had every reason to treat us very well in connection with trade agreements. I shall quote briefly from the final part of the letter as follows:
I am- authorized to put forward the following outline as a suitable basis for the negotiation of a trade agreement:
(a)	A mutual undertaking to maintain during the lifetime of the agreement the unrestricted free entry of commodities now on the free list of either country.
(b)	The mutual concession of tariff treatment as favourable as that accorded to any other foreign country;
That is the gist of that paragraph.
(c)	The reduction by 50 per cent of the existing United States rates of duty, as authorized by the Tariff Act of 1934, on a specified
number of natural products, including inter alia, lumber, fish, potatoes, milk and cream, and live cattle; a number of other agricultural products, and several minerals both metallic and non-metallic.
That, in brief, is the gist of the letter; and if you will note, Mr. Speaker, at no page or paragraph of that letter did we offer to give up our preferences in the United Kingdom. That, to my mind, is one of the chief points of difference between our proposal to the United States government and the attitude taken by the present government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: May I point out to my hon. friend that neither did we, with regard to our first treaty.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I quite agree, but you did with regard to this treaty, and this is the one I am discussing.
To prove again that the Conservative party is favourable to trade I am going to read the plank of the Conservative party adopted at its national convention last July. It has a direct bearing on the present discussion, because, of course, it was known at that time that the trade treaty was being negotiated, and I suppose the negotiations had some bearing on the drafting of this resolution. It is a little lengthy, but I will read the whole of it because I think it should be on record both for us and for our friends opposite. It is the trade and commerce resolution passed in July at the National Liberal-no, not Liberal; I was going to say Liberal-Conservative, but they changed the name of the party to National Conservative, and I have not quite got used to it yet. This is the plank:
This National Conservative convention declares its continued adherence to its traditional policy of fostering and sustaining by fiscal protection Canadian labour and Canadian industries, and especially the primary industries of agriculture, fisheries, forestry and mining, all of which are essential to the maintenance of a well-balanced national economy, while, at the same time, guarding against undue advantage being taken of the protection so afforded.
It also affirms its adherence to the underlying principles of that policy, which have served to stimulate the development of the natural resources of Canada, to preserve and to enlarge the domestic markets for Canadian products, to promote interprovincial trade, and, generally, to provide a diversified economic life which will serve to retain Canada's sons and daughters within our own boundaries.
This convention affirms the policy of having tariff schedules under scientific investigation by a permanent tariff commission and that, in case it is ascertained that unfair advantage is being taken of any customs duties imposed by such schedules, the tariff commission shall

Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement
m-ke recommendations, to which effect shall be given by the government, for reducing such r?fes of duty or for removing them from the tariff schedules.
That is very important, and I have so stated on many occasions on public platforms. In other words, it is the plank against exploitation behind tariff walls. We established the tariff board on that very basis, as my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Stewart) reminds me.
I continue with the resolution:
This convention affirms its firm adherence to the policy of preferential trade within the British commonwealth of nations, by which Canada obtained the boon of tariff preferences in the markets of the United Kingdom and of other dominions, and which have served to mitigate the severity of the trade depression during recent years, and which were approved by parliament, despite the bitter, determined and prolonged opposition of the Liberal party.
This convention is convinced that the permanent. interests of Canada are best conserved by enlarging our markets in the United Kingdom and in other British dominions, whose products are more complementary than competitive with those of this country, and with which our trade agreements are more likely to be durable and beneficial.
Then this last paragraph:
This convention believes that the external trade of Canada may also be increased advantageously by the negotiation, on a fair and equitable basis, of trade agreements with countries which are outside of the British Empire, but that in negotiations with foreign countries, the terms agreed upon should not be such as to impair the benefits derived by Canada under existing agreements between Canada and the United Kingdom and between Canada and other British dominions.
It seems to me, sir, that that resolution is proof sufficient that the Conservative party is not a party of economic nationalism, and that all of us believe in trade.
The Prime Minister claimed, and the Liberal party have been claiming, that this treaty helps to foster world peace and the unity of the democracies of the world.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Some of my hon. friends opposite, I think about half a dozen, applaud.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

speechtext: I was speaking of this treaty in conjunction with the United Kingdom-United States agreement.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman talked as if this was not a trade treaty but a peace treaty. As I listened to him, I thought he spoke, as if we had just been engaged in a spectacular war with some great nation and had won a glorious victory; and
[Mr. Maniou.J
as I waited for his peroration I watched, as an hon. gentleman watched me on another occasion, to see the victims come marching up through the aisles of parliament. He spoke as if we had won some great victory, and yet, as I pointed out the other night, not since 1812, a period of over a hundred years, have we had any differences of a serious nature with the United States, and certainly since the beginning of the century there have been no differences between Great Britain and the United States. It is true, I admit, that prior to the beginning of this century, there were those in the United States who occasionally twisted the lion's tail, as the phrase was at that time, but since the end of the last century so far as I know there has been no attempt, except perhaps by an occasional individual, to do anything of that kind. Yet it looked to m.e as if the Prime Minister were trying to point out in his address to the house the other day, and indeed he implied this in his interruption a moment ago, that this treaty meant a great advance towards peace throughout the world. On occasion the right hon. gentleman can attain heights of oratory on matters of that sort, even if, as now, he is imagining most of what he says. I well remember, and I thought of it as the right hon. gentleman spoke the other day, an expression used by an old friend of his, and incidentally of mine, the late Right Hon. W. S. Fielding, but not with reference to the Prime Minister. He said that a certain gentleman on the other side of the house could make a hogshead of lather out of an ounce of soap. I could not help but think of the expression when the right hon. gentleman got so much worked up the other day on this question. I envy him at times when he does that sort of thing. I am not able to do it. I am just a plain, blunt man who sticks to the facts. I do not use language-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: My hon. friend does not need any soap at all to make a lather.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
My hon. friends opposite are pretty slippery with the soap they do use. I use language to express my thoughts, not to hide them. And so I suggest that all of us, including even the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, should keep our feet on the ground and not get our heads up among the clouds. After all, we are but eleven millions of people and we are not so powerful a factor in the peace of the world as some of us seem to think. Let us be realists, not weavers of words or dreamers of dreams.
I want to emphasize the fact that all of us in this great dominion are friendly to the United States. The majority of the people

Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement
in our two countries speak the same language, and have the same traditions, the same customs, the same laws. We understand each other. For the people of the United States we entertain most friendly feelings. I admit frankly that in common with other afterdinner speakers I have often boasted of Canada and the United States living peacefully side by side for over a hundred years, without serious quarrels or disputes, as an example to the world of which we may well be proud. In that connection I want to take exception to one thing which the right hon. gentleman said about me in his speech, in the debate on the address. He referred to me as if I had spoken of the president of the United States. But I would point out that I did not mention the president of the United States at all. What I said was that after the Munich agreement all I heard coming from the United States-these were my words, and perhaps they were not quite as definite as they should have been-was criticism of Chamberlain. I was referring to writers, and to such magazines as Time, a very fine magazine which I read regularly and like very much, but which makes me see as red as its cover by its articles against Chamberlain and the settlement which the Bi'itish and the French made at Munich. Indeed, since I spoke on the address, a professor from one of the United States universities made a speech in Montreal quite critical of Mr. Chamberlain, and along the same lines. The reason I mention it-

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I do not think that my hon. friend caught the significance of my remark. I did not think he had reflected on the president; rather I thought he had forgotten altogether the president's contribution.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I was not speaking of the president; I was speaking of the populace generally. The right hon. gentleman is more careful to-day than he was the other day. I have the quotation here, and I think I had better read it so that there can be no misinterpretation:
I was rather surprised this afternoon to hear what my hon. friend had to say about the actions of the President of the United States at the time of the crisis last year.
That is on page 58 of Hansard. On page 59 he said:
I say to my hon. friend that if he had given that quotation to the house-
He had quoted Mr. Chamberlain.
-instead of saying what he did, he would have been more patriotic in his attitude. I can conceive of nothing less patriotic in these times than an effort on the part of any Canadian public man or citizen to try to create prejudices between this country and the United States.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend that the actions of the president which I there referred to were the all important communications that he sent to Germany and to other countries. My hon. friend's remark was to the effect that nothing had come out of the United States except criticism.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I admit that I was a little indefinite and probably did not make my point clear, but the right hon. gentleman had no right to apply to me statements about the president of the United States which I had not made, and he had much less right-I mention this very seriously to-day-to question my patriotism. I do not question the patriotism of anybody in this house: I say this very seriously. I take it for granted that we are all good, loyal, patriotic Canadians. I am not going to question anybody's patriotism, but I object very strongly to anybody questioning mine. Probably that will be sufficient to say regarding that matter. The reason I mention it at all is that it was misinterpreted in England. I had a letter from a friend who said he had read a report of my speech in the London Daily Telegraph, and he added, "Until I read your speech in Hansard-with every word of which I agree- 1 was under the impression, gained from the report of the Prime Minister's remarks, that you had said things which were not very wise."
In closing the incident I just suggest this, that we should all bear in mind in discussing foreign relations of any kind that these international relations are too important and too delicate to be made a football of politics, and that we should avoid anything in the way of taking, even though we have the opportunity, political advantage from them.
Let me say further about the President of the United States that nobody more than our group welcomed the words of the president at Ivy Lea, when he said in effect that the United States would come to the relief of Canada if Canada were attacked.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It was at
Queens university, Kingston.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I beg pardon: it was the same day the bridge was opened at Ivy Lea. We should remember, however, that the president's statement had no reference to trade. To my mind it was a statement of the position of the United States with regard to its own self-defence. It is to prevent a flank attack upon the United States that the United States so frankly takes this attitude. Ever since the Monroe doctrine was declared, over one hundred years ago, the United States has taken the same attitude The Monroe

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
doctrine forbids any European country which was not then already settled, in a sense, on this continent from becoming settled here; and I have no doubt that if Mr. Roosevelt were asked he would say that he would go just as quickly to the defence of Mexico, were Mexico attacked by some foreign country, as he would to the defence of Canada. As I say, that would be done for the purpose of self-defence, because the Americans do not want Japan, Germany, Italy or any other country to get a foothold in Canada or Mexico and thereby to gain a side-door entrance to the United States. The president's statement had nothing whatever to do with trade. I say also that the friendship of the democracies has nothing to do with trade. Great Britain and France, Canada and the other British dominions, and the United States are and should remain friendly, and I think will remain friendly, because they have the same ideals of individual freedom, much the same parliamentary institutions, and largely the same economic system. These democracies all desire peace. The peoples who are endangering the peace of the world at the present time are not the democracies but the dictatorships. I venture to say that if future wars were dependent upon the actions of the democracies the world would never again be cursed with war.
To support my attitude may I make one or two quotations? I took this out of the Ottawa Journal yesterday afternoon: it is dated February 15, from Washington:
The House of Representatives heard sales of United States airplanes abroad defended to-day on the ground that "Americans are safe only so long as England and France stand."
That is what one congressman said. A little further down:
Representative Pace, democrat, Georgia, member of the house military committee, told the house that he thought it was sound to aid Great Britain and France build up their defences because if those democracies fell before the dictatorships a major bulwark of the United States would be removed.
"Is it not better," he said, "to sell England and France planes for their defence than to go to war with a big power to prevent an encroachment on this hemisphere?"
Asserting that the United States "for selfish reasons" would be forced, defensively, to go to the aid of Canada or Great Britain in an emergency, Pace added, "I feel sure that the President did not say 'Our frontier is on the Rhine'. In my judgment he could well have said, 'Our first line defence is England and France'. When we see England and France go down, we are threatened."
That is an American view of the whole situation. I think it is a perfectly proper and correct view. And that is the reason; not trade treaties, not trade, not dollars and

cents; but the freedom of democracy, the belief in democracy, is the reason that the United States is ready if necessary to help, in various ways, countries like the United Kingdom, France and Canada, in case of difficulty.
With regard to international appeasement, we all want it. We want it just as much as we want peace. But appeasement, like charity, begins at home. We have not appeasement, at least we have not peace, in our own country to-day because of economic conditions, unemployment, lack of opportunity, insecurity, all of which are so common throughout Canada at the present time. To my mind-and I shall try to prove it before I conclude-this agreement increases those detrimental economic conditions and therefore lessens the possibility of our having peace and appeasement in our own country.
A few moments ago I quoted an American. I am now going to quote a prominent British public man, in regard to this treaty, to show that the British are not putting up any verbal fog to try to confuse the people. They are talking of the two trade agreements, merely as business arrangements. Mr. Oliver Stanley, president of the board of trade, who occupies the same position in Great Britain as the Minister of Trade and Commerce does in Canada, speaking at a luncheon of the Canadian chamber of commerce in London a few days after these agreements were signed, made this statement;
"You may ask what about the political effects of the agreements," said Mr. Stanley. "The fact is I have never looked upon this as a political treaty. I have looked upon it entirely as an economic bargain."
That is his attitude. It is the attitude I am taking, and it is the attitude I think we should all take. It is not a matter of politics so far as the agreements are concerned; it is a matter of business.
Here is another quotation from the same speech of his, and I think it is worth putting on Hansard although it has not any connection with the immediate statement that I have made:
It was natural in trade matters, he said, that "we should consider our own interests first and the empire next."
In other words, he was looking at it from the straight point of view of business-the proper attitude. No criticism is implied in my quoting that. A week later, on November 28, he made another speech. Joseph Kennedy, the United States ambassador to the court of St. James, was present. Here are two more quotations from Mr. Stanley's speech in reference to the new

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
Anglo-American trade agreement. True, he was not referring to the Canada-United States treaty, but his conclusion applies.
Mr. Stanley, praising it as "wide and fair," said Great Britain concluded the pact without political aims.
That is clear. I want my right hon. friend particularly, and some of his followers, to mark the next clause:
"It takes in more than 600 items," he said, "but one item we did not include was 'eyewash.' We think it is eminently fair to both sides and to the world."
I suggest that the eyewash might be left out in Canada as well as in England. Let me quote another British opinion. The Right Hon. L. S. Amery, speaking at the annual meeting of the Empire Industries Association on November 29, 1938, ten days after .the treaty was signed, made a statement which was quoted in the London Times of November 30, 1938. I quote:
Mr. Amery begged leave to be a little skeptical about the claim that this treaty was a contribution towards international trade and goodwill. He suggested that it would not have the slightest effect on the policy of totalitarianism or on economic nationalism in other countries, and he frankly believed that as a contribution to the opening of the trade doors of the world it was more imaginary than real. The Ottawa agreements-
-that is, the empire trade agreements of 1932- were intended to be the first steps in a forward policy for the development of interempire trade. It seemed to Mr. Amery that any further steps in that direction were forbidden in almost every, direction by the Anglo-American treaty.
That is as far as I shall go in discussing that aspect of the question. I submit that the talk about this treaty as having anything whatever to do with world peace is simply what Mr. Oliver Stanley called it, "eyewash."
There is another point I should like to touch upon at this juncture. In his speech the Prime Minister apparently objected to my describing the Canadian newspaper release as ballyhoo and propaganda. Well, there were forty-three pages in the press release, and if it was not ballyhoo and propaganda, some of it at any rate was deceptive. I find that the people's money is being used for the spreading of political propaganda about this treaty. I have here a page of the Toronto Star of February 7, 1939, ten days ago, over half of which is taken up with a paid advertisement signed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) and by the deputy minister-an advertisement paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. To my mind it is largely Liberal propaganda. For example, in large print there appears this statement:
New trade agreements are further encouragements to Canadian exporters.
That may be correct; I will not argue at the moment about the possible facts. I do not understand, however, why the people of Canada should be asked to pay for such advertisements, and I use the word " advertisements" advisedly, because I do not doubt the hon. gentleman had it printed in other newspapers. I do not suppose^ he limited it to the Toronto Star. I do not see why the Canadian people should pay for putting out Liberal propaganda.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Any more than they should pay for Tory propaganda published by the former Minister of Trade and Commerce.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman can take that up when he speaks. That should not have been paid for either if it was paid for by the government. I do not know about it. There was some criticism, my colleague the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) says, but I do not remember the incident. I say frankly that it should not have been paid for.
The Prime Minister pointed out that the trade agreements favoured the democracies; but they also favour the autocracies, because through the most favoured nation clauses, countries like Japan, Germany, Italy and even Russia are favoured by the agreement. At any rate they are favoured indirectly, and that without giving any return to Canada. For example, Russia and the Argentine are favoured, because when you take off the six cent preference on wheat which was favourable to Canada you give Russia and the Argentine the same advantages in the British market as you give to the United States. Since the war, in one or two periods at least, Russia has been a large exporter and yet, under the treaty, we give to that country the same advantage without gaining any return.
Trade treaties are not necessarily peace guarantors. Austria had a trade treaty with Germany just before Hitler walked in and took possession. As a matter of fact, there are in all trade treaties the seeds of disharmony. I do not intend to quote many passages from the agreement, but from pages one to ten I find a number of indefinite terms, terms so indefinite indeed that they might well lead to misunderstanding. For example:
In those cases in which the other country is a relatively large supplier of any such article . . .
And again:
. . . the commerce of the other country shall receive fair and equitable treatment.
Whose judgment is to be final in deciding this question? With regard to sawn lumber and timber this phrase is used: " In substantial
Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement

quantities." But what are substantial quantities? Who is to determine that question? As I say, it might lead to disputes. Again:
If a wide variation should occur in the rate of exchange . . .
What is a wide variation? Does a wide variation exist to-day? To what extent must the rates vary to constitute a wide variation? These are examples of many expressions that are to be found in the treaty, which are open to dispute and which might lead to serious differences of opinion. I admit that it is not a very grave matter, but it might develop into something serious. A trade treaty might well lead to differences instead of bringing about understanding and harmony.
I suggest that the Liberals are trying to float this treaty through on a flood of propaganda. After all, I repeat, the United States is our chief competitor in wheat, fruits, meat and lumber. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking on the address, made the statement that the United States now recognizes British preferences.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The minister says, "Hear, hear." Have we reached the stage where the United States has to recognize British preferences? Is that to be regarded as another step beyond that taken by the Prime Minister in 1929, I believe, when he said that in trade matters we must do nothing to provoke the United States? Is it another manifestation of the same attitude taken by the right hon. gentleman at that time? Certainly it does seem strange to me.
Let me give briefly some of the chief objections to the treaty as I view it, because I cannot help the feeling that we have given up the British substance for the American shadow. Briefly, these are my principal objections to the treaty:
1.	It makes for greater competition with our industries which are very much the same as those of the United States.
2.	It affords concessions to thirty-one favoured nations which give nothing in return.
3.	It brings unfair competition from favoured nations such as Japan, Germany, Italy, as a result of low standards of living and low wages, and the loss of all liberties to labour in those countries, without returning anything to Canada.
4.	It is the beginning of the destruction of the whole British preferential system for which we have been struggling since 1897 and which we accomplished in the British trade agreements of 1932.
5.	It cuts into the British markets, our best markets in wheat, fruits, lumber, and so on.
[Mr. Monion. 1
6.	It injures our Canadian traffic and damages the transportation system, railways, steamships and so forth, sending traffic north and south instead of east and west.
7.	It gives too much in return for too little; in other words, it is not an equalization of favours.
8.	It will probably lessen revenues through the elimination of the three per cent special excise tax and the lowering of other tariffs.
9.	It will probably increase unemployment through greater competition with industries such as coal, mining, manufacturing and so on.
Why is it that we get the worst of it in this agreement? There are a number of reasons. In the first place, the United States tariffs were and are much higher than ours. They have always been; they have been much more highly protected in the United States than we have been, their tariffs starting higher up than ours and not having to come down as low. The United States duty against wheat, for example, was 42 cents a bushel; our duty against their wheat is 12 cents. The Prime Minister himself pointed out that if the wheat duty into the United States were cut in two, from 42 cents to 21 cents, it would not be of very much use to the Canadian wheat grower for the reason that 21 cents would still be too high a tariff oyer which to ship Canadian wheat. That is all the president of the United States could do-cut the tariff in half. That is the second reason why we got the worst of it; the maximum cut the president could make, according to the act of 1934, was fifty per cent of the tariff, whereas we could and in some cases did take away altogether the tariff against United States products.
Third, they are shrewder traders than we are. I had the word "sharper" in my notes, but I do not like to use it because it might be taken as offensive, and I do not mean it in that way. The down-east Yankee spirit is strong in the United States, and incidentally I like the down-east Yankees, so I am not using that phrase offensively. The hon. gentleman to my right says they out-smart us, and I think they do.
Fourth, the United States has only nineteen favoured nations which automatically get the favours that they give Canada, while we have thirty-one favoured nations.
Fifth, their producers had the opportunity of appearing before the committee for reciprocity information, which is in the nature of a tariff board, to register opposition to the negotiation of a treaty that would affect them. That opportunity was not afforded Canadian producers in this country. I hold in my hand a Department of State press release of January,, 28, 1938, a little over a year ago, when

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
this treaty was under negotiation. It is marked, "Confidential release for publication in the morning newspapers of Saturday, January 29," and contains these words:
The Secretary of State issued to-day formal notice of intention to negotiate a new trade agreement with the government of Canada.
Here are the two paragraphs that illustrate the fact that the producers in the United States had an opportunity to appear before some authority, while ours did not:
Pursuant to section 4 of an act of congress approved June 12, 1934, entitled "An act to amend the Tariff Act of 1930," as extended by public resolution No. 10, approved March 1, 1937, and to executive order No. 6750, of June 27, 1934, I hereby give notice of intention to negotiate a trade agreement with the government of Canada.
This is the next paragraph:
All presentations of information and views in writing, and applications for supplemental oral presentation of views with respect to the negotiation of such agreement should be submitted to the committee for reciprocity information in accordance with the announcement of this date issued by that committee concerning the manner and dates for the submission of briefs and applications, and the time set for public hearing.
That is signed by Mr. Cordell Hull. I think this should be on record. What has happened as a result of this opportunity being afforded in the United States, together with the fact that they are shrewder traders than we are? With regard to very many products the duties in the United States are much higher since the negotiation of this treaty than the same duties in the reverse direction, that is, in Canada. It is true that there are a few items where the opposite is true, but there are not very many; I hunted for them. Take the case of bacon, hams, shoulders and other pork products. The duty in Canada is If cents per pound; the duty in the United States is 2 cents per pound. The duty on potatoes entering Canada is 374 cents per hundred pounds for six weeks, from June 15 to July 31, and for the remainder of the year they enter free. The duty in the United States is 374 cents from March to November and 60 cents from December to February. On carrots, radishes and cauliflower there is a ten per cent duty on importations from the United States and a 25 per cent duty on United States importations from Canada. On asparagus and spinach there is a 10 per cent duty this way and a 50 per cent duty the other way. On tomatoes our duty is 14 cents and the United States duty is 3 cents.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: That does not take into account our valuations, which form a very important part of our tariff system.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I do not suppose that takes into account their valuations either.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: They do not have them.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: These are the rates now in force, and I do not suppose there is any reason to suspect that our valuations are higher than theirs, in proportion.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It is a different system altogether.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
On mackerel, for example, to take one of the many fish items, the duty is 4 cent per pound into Canada and from 1 to 14 cents into the United States, depending on whether the fish are fresh or frozen. Wheat, as I have already said, carries a duty of 12 cents entering Canada and 42 cents entering the United States. I have various clothing items here also. On clothing of which silk is the main component the duty is 30 per cent in Canada and 65 per cent in the United States. On clothing of which artificial silk is the main component the duty is 324 per cent entering Canada and 45 cents per pound and 65 per cent going into the United States. In view of all this boasting with regard to the effects of this treaty I ask why Canada's duties on the vast majority of these items should be lower than the duties on the same commodities entering the United States.
During the debate on the address I presented an argument which I should like to repeat now, that the United States is and always has been an uncertain market for Canada. I think the Prime Minister mentioned the reciprocity treaty of 1854, which was cancelled very abruptly in 1866, and earlier in my speech I quoted Sir Wilfrid Laurier's words about "no more pilgrimages to W ashingtOn." I presume he was referring to that very treaty. I have also put on record the fact that in 1922 the United States imposed the Fordney-McCumber tariff and in 1930 the Hawley-Smoot tariff against our products. It may be said that those tariffs applied to all the world, but we were a big exporter to the United States, and this was done at a time when we were importing almost twice as much as they were buying from us. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce said my comparison of $11 per capita as against $1 per capita was not fair. I am not going to argue the point; I do not think it matters very much, because I did not mean to be unfair, but surely it would be reasonable to compare one nation with the other. Surely the United States with 130,000,000 people should buy as much from us as we, with 11,000,000 people, buy from them.
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

Yet, sir, in the decade from 1921 to 1930 our trade with the United States showed a balance against us of 8287,000,000 per year.
It seems to me the United States have always been rather harsh towards us, in view of the fact that we are their best customers. Writing in the Foreign Affairs Journal of October, 1929, Professor Taussig of Harvard used these words:
For many years we have treated Canada much as a big bully treats the smaller boy.
In my opinion that was demonstrated by the Lumber Marking Act of 1938. At that time we had a trade treaty which had been negotiated by the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues, which included lumber; yet the United States put through this marking act which, our lumbermen complained, prevented by a roundabout method our lumber from entering the United States.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Has that not been removed?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Yes, it has; but for some months it was in force, and all the lumbermen who spoke to me about it at the time, long before this treaty was negotiated, pointed out that the very fact that each piece of lumber had marked on it "Produced in Canada" prevented a great deal of our lumber from entering the United States.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It came into force on September 1 of last year.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Yes, and was cancelled some months later.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It was
cancelled when the new treaty was signed.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It was in effect only for two or three months, but in my opinion that was an unfair method of dealing with our lumbermen, and that is all I am pointing out.
Then there is the cattle quota. In the press release of my right hon. friend and his government it was stated that we had a cattle quota of something like 225,000 head -I think that is the correct figure-to be shipped into the United States. And we thought we had. Now, it is discovered that that is what the United States calls a global quota-that is, it refers to the whole world, and does not refer to Canada alone. As a matter of fact, in the first quarter of this year we learned that instead of our having the right to ship into the United States 60,000 head of cattle, Mexico shipped in 45 per cent of that 60,000, and that is cut off from our cattle quota. Why?
My right hon. friend objected to my using the word "propaganda". He objected to my

using the word "ballyhoo". I say now that if the fact which was mentioned in the release, namely that we have a quota of 60,000 head, is not ballyhoo or propaganda, then it is deception-and I think it is deception. I should have used the word "deception" to the people of Canada.
Until the other day-I discovered it I believe-we did not know that part of the quota was given to Mexico.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Do they know?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I had a letter from
western Canada, but I shall deal with it later on. There is another point I should like to make about the unfair results of the treaty. Il is this rather extraordinary thing which was shown in the press release. Our new reductions to the United States number 283 items, whereas their new reductions to us number 129-considerably less than half.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Items do not mean anything; it depends upon the amount involved.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Apparently nothing means anything to my hon. friend. I am speaking of the items and, as I say, so far as I can see, the United' States is getting two to one, from this government. I am asking myself: Why should they?
The government claims that the six cent preference on wheat we were given in the empire trade agreements was of no use. They have said that this preference was of no particular value to us. Well, perhaps it does not matter to a farmer in the west to-day because he has obtained a guarantee of eighty cent wheat, so he is not worried. But I say that every bushel of United States wheat which goes over there to replace our wheat is just that much more competition against us. And it is a most dangerous type of competition because it replaces our wheat and shows the British consumer that United States wheat is as good as ours-or almost as good. There is not much No. 1 hard; it is mostly No. 1 northern; and the northern United States produce good wheat. In addition to that, as I pointed out, Russia and the Argentine, without giving anything in return, get the same advantage. If Russia achieves an exporting position for wheat, she has the same advantage.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that the United States government was subsidizing wheat up to seventeen cents a bushel, and that since this new agreement has passed they have agreed not to subsidize the wheat growers in the United States, on the British market?

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I do not know whether they have agreed to that. I did see the item in the press to that effect. I shall deal with that in a few moments.
It seems to me that if the United States is subsidizing United States wheat, that is all the more reason why we should retain our preference. If it is not another advantage to the United States to have the preference of six cents a bushel removed, then why is the United States so jubilant over it? In their official publications they have been jubilant. I shall quote two items of their press release regarding wheat. These are their views in regard to the six cent preference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: And the opposition down there calls that document ballyhoo.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I assume there is a certain amount of ballyhoo about it, too. I admit we are not the only people who play politics. But at the same time this is the statement in their press release. It was not distributed by the government of Canada. I happened to get this from the United States office. Here is what they have to say about grain, at page 6:
One of the most important concessions is the removal of the duty on wheat, which has been equivalent to about six cents per bushel. This has tended to divert trade to Canada and Australia. The United States formerly sold great quantities of wheat to the United Kingdom and with normal crops in the future and the restoration of free entry it should again be able to sell large quantities. Also, as a result of the removal of the preference, it should be possible for American port and transportation interests to regain their lost business in the transhipment of Canadian wheat to the United Kingdom.
I agree with that. I used that argument before I saw that statement; I believe I used it in my speech on the address in reply.
Then, at page 19 of the same release they say the following-and this is the proof of the pudding, so to speak:
Grain and grain products.
Wheat: The granting of duty-free treatment for wheat by the United Kingdom should prove of marked value to American wheat growers and the American wheat export trade. The import duty on non-empire wheat has been at the rate of 2 shillings per 480 pounds since November 17, 1932.
That is, the six cents a bushel.
A duty of this size (about six cents per bushel) applicable to wheat from some countries and not others often is sufficient to divert the trade.
Then they go on:
The concession of free entry for American wheat should benefit also the American transportation and port business. In order to obtain the benefits of the United Kingdom 71492-67
preference, Canadian wheat, which formerly moved in large quantities through American ports has under the preference been shipped principally to the United Kingdom direct from Canadian ports. In view of this concession, American port and transportation interests will be in a position to reenter the transshipment business.
The United Kingdom is the leading wheat-import market of the world. Formerly about a fourth of the total American wheat exports were regularly shipped to the United Kingdom. Under the influence of the world economic depression and the establishment of an import duty in 1932-*
Get this.
Under the influence of the world economic depression and the establishment of an import duty in 1932-
That is what we got.	*
"-(with empire wheat remaining duty free), imports of American wheat into the United Kingdom dropped from 39,267,000 bushels in 1930 (20-1 per cent of total wheat imports) to only 9,000 bushels in 1933-

-while imports from empire sources for the corresponding years rose from 79,234,000 bushels (40-5 per cent of total wheat imports) to 140,459,000 bushels (07-0 per cent of the total).

Well now, the very figures of the imports given by them as a proof of the injury done to the United States wheat grower by the six cent preference on Canadian wheat shows the correctness of the argument that the United States was injured and that we were benefited by that preference.
Then, I have here an item from Boston, appearing in the Telegraph-Journal of St. John on January 20, 1939:
First Canadian wheat to move through the port of Boston to British markets in more than two years, a shipment of 24,000 bushels will be placed in the steamship Newfoundland on Saturday for delivery at Liverpool.
Earlier this month a shipment of 280,000 bushels of Canadian wheat moved through this port to Rotterdam. Shipment of Canadian grain through Boston follows the removal in the United Kingdom-United States trade treaty of the six cents a bushel preference on grain shipped to Great Britain through Canadian ports.
That is clear. I do not think the matter is debatable. Then there is another item from the Dow Jones agency of New York showing

105S
Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement

that they expected the same occurence to take place, namely that the ports of Canada would be hurt and the United States ports helped.
I have here another item-from the Christian Science Monitor of November 18- of which I shall read only one paragraph:
"As a result of the removal of the preference," a state department announcement said, "it should be possible for American port and transportation interests to regain their lost business in the transshipment of Canadian wheat to the United Kingdom."
Those facts seem to me unanswerable. It is not a case of an opinion; the facts are there. I have in my hand an article sent to me by a practical grain man of the city of Montreal. This is a statement which appeared on February 3, 1938, a year ago. I take it it was prepared by the shipping interests in Canada. They point out something which is quite true, that while there was nothing in the empire trade agreements that forced Canadian wheat through Canadian ports in order to get the preference, the fact was that the British customs regulations actually forced our wheat to go through our ports. I shall read just a brief summary from this document.
