speechtext:
It is not signed. I shall
pass it over to the hon. gentleman when I have finished. It reads:
If the preference is lifted or varied which it can be done by the United Kingdom customs the Canadian interests affected are:
1.	Canadian lower lake elevator interests, as storage and transfer will naturally flow again through U.S. lake and Atlantic ports.
2.	Canadian lake carriers, as with shipments via Buffalo-Atlantic ports, American ships can carry to Buffalo and will do so, as next season's outlook is for restricted traffic of American products for the American lake carrier.
3.	Canadian railroads, as they would lose the bay-Montreal haul during navigation season, and Montreal-Saint John, Halifax during winter seasons.
4.	Canadian labour on Canadian ships, railways and in elevators, et cetera.
It may be said that this is exaggerated, but I do not think so. Naturally those who are interested do not want to be injured by this treaty, and they published this pamphlet. As I said, I do not know just who published it, but it was sent to me by a prominent grain man in Montreal as their argument. Here are some interesting figures. In 1931 the empire countries shipped 42-6 of the wheat sent into the United Kingdom. That was

before the empire trade agreements. In 1938, empire countries shipped in 63-2 per cent. In 1931 foreign countries shipped in 57-4 per cent, and in 1938, 36-8 per cent. Those figures illustrate what happened as a result of the empire trade agreements.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Those are percentages of
what?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I am sorry if I did not
make myself clear. They are percentages of wheat imports into the British market. I have here a statement published by the economic branch of the Royal Bank of Canada. This has nothing particular to do with the trade treaty, but it sets out a few facts which I take for granted are correct. They point out that woidd wheat production for the current season is placed at the record total of 4,459 million bushels. They give the supplies available for export as 1,135 million bushels. They point out that importers' requirements are only 550 million bushels and therefore, there will be a carry-over of something like 1,000 million bushels. This illustrates the need for markets for our Canadian wheat, and that is why I mention it. They go on to say:
International demand for wheat declined from a peak of 947 million bushels in 1928-29 to 523 million in 1935-36. Since that time little improvement has been evident, total shipments amounting to 609 million bushels in 1936-37 and 512 million in 1937-38.
Then they go on to point out that the only stable market that remains-"static" is the word I used a while ago-is the British market. They continue:
In Argentina, however, conditions were much more favourable during the latter part of the season and a bumper crop was harvested. The first official estimate places the outturn at 316 million bushels, the largest on record with the exception of that harvested in 1928-29, and compares with 185 million bushels harvested in 1937-38.
They point out that the Argentine harvest is double what it was a year previously. Despite that fact, w'e are taking this treaty method of losing some of our markets. We are losing our six cent preference, and yet there is more wheat to be shipped by countries like the Argentine, whose crop is double this year what it was last year. All this is going to make matters more difficult for the Canadian producer. I submit that our preferences are being destroyed. I have many quotations here, and I shall read briefly from a few. An apple producer writes to say:
United States requires the export market only for her surplus production; Canada requires it for almost , half her production.

Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement
I quote from the Seattle Post-Intelligencer of November 18, 1938, as follows:
This is a start in bringing back our export business to the United Kingdom. The previous tax of 45 cents per box for apples was prohibitive. The reduction, approximating 15 cents per box is still inadequate, but it will help.
The Business Week of New York of November 26, 1938. states:
The British pact is more important diplomatically, but the biggest trade concessions are made in the Canadian pact.
The two new pacts, while they do not wipe out the system of empire preferences which was set up at Ottawa in 1932, mark the first important move to break down that system.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) was inquiring about subsidies paid by the United States, and in this connection I quote from the Ottawa Citizen of December 5, 1938:
British millers who bought 20,000,000 bushels of wheat from the United States made this a condition of their purchase of the grain
U. S. to prevent further exports of subsidized flour to Great Britain
British millers have purchased approximately 20,000.000 bushels of United States wheat through ordinary commercial channels. The cost was $13,750,000.
Shipments will begin in January when the wheat duty is lifted and continue over six months.
Just because of the destruction of the preference. Then I quote from the New York Times of November 18, 1938, a Washington dispatch dated November' 17:
The reciprocal trade agreement between the United States and Great Britain, which was signed here to-day, may well have sounded the death knell of the empire preference theory of trade among the members of the British empire. This system, which was advocated by Lord Beaverbrook and others in London, was put into actual effect by the Ottawa agreements, signed late in 1932 and renewed in modified form last year.
And again:
In the agreement signed to-day, several imperial preferences have been extended to include the United States. That is to say, produce of the United States may enter Great Britain at the same rate as competitive produce from some of the dominions, whereas previously the American goods had to pay a higher import duty than similar goods from an empire source.
If the six cents preference on wheat going into the British market was of no use to us, why are all these different sources in the United States so jubilant over its removal? 71492-67J
Here is another dispatch from Washington-dated November 17, appearing in the same issue of the New York Times:
Now, because both Canadian and American, wheat are, by virtue of the British trade agreement, on the same duty-free basis, Canadian wheat may pass through American ports if its shippers desire.
Officials said this would prove a great boon to American railroads, transfer workers and shipping.
I shall quote from one British source. Thf London Economist of November 26 has this
to say:
It is more questionable whether there will be a corresponding increase in British imports. Very few of the concessions made to the United States will result in any category of American goods being placed in a more favourable competitive position vis-a-vis the domestic producer. Most of the agricultural products affected are not grown in this country, or where they are, the domestic producer is already safeguarded.
Listen to these words.
In these eases the effect of the agreement will largely be to divert a certain quantity of trade from dominion (largely Canadian) to American hands, without increasing the total volume of imports.
I ask again what I asked a few moments ago. Where is the advantage if we lose some of our trade and the United States gets it? World trade remains the same, but ours does not. What is the advantage to the world? I cannot see it myself. I simply say, Mr. Speaker, that the United States cares for its own people when it is making a trade treaty of this kind. This government is too anxious for a trade agreement. It wants trade agreements at any price. I say now, from all the mail I am getting from all over this country, that very many of our people, producers of one kind and another-and I have had letters from dozens of different types of producers, agricultural and manufacturing-are very much opposed to this treaty. They protest against it as damaging to them. But they are afraid to protest openly because they know that the budget is going to be brought down in this house probably within a month, and if they protest openly they are just a little afraid of what might happen to them. So the industrialists, the producers, and the workers in the plants or industries affected are afraid to express their viewpoint.
Let me deal briefly with fruits and vegetables, and this will illustrate what has been done to some of our agriculturists. Before 1936 the duty on fruits coming into Canada was 20 per cent, and on vegetables 30 per cent. The duty on both is now down to 10 per cent, as a result -of this treaty and the treaty of 1935. Our season for the production
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

*of fruit and vegetables is much later than the season in the United States, and so it is [DOT]difficult for our farmers to produce fruits and vegetables in competition with United States production. I take this attitude, that so far as possible our growers should have the first opportunity in our market.
Then, as I pointed out about apples, the United States sells only its surplus abroad. It has a huge market within its borders, and now it can dump whatever surplus it has much more cheaply into the British market because of the removal of part of the preference, whereas our Canadian producers, with our small population, have to sell about half their apple production in other countries, mostly in Great Britain.
. I have also had strong protests from our tomato growers, some of whom say it is going to ruin their industry. They point 'out that under the treaty there is a duty of H cents a pound on United States tomatoes entering Canada and a duty of 3 cents a pound on Canadian tomatoes entering the United States.
There is another industry, the British Columbia door industry, that is going to be affected adversely by this treaty. There called at my office a few days ago a gentleman who lias for many years been associated indirectly with that industry. I do not wish to give his aiame, but he is an outstanding student as well as a business man. He came into my office and gave me this information. I have confirmed it with British Columbia people.
He says that the door industry in British Columbia began in 1933, after we obtained the preference on doors in the British market. I will read the data he gave me just as I jotted it down. Until 1933 Canada had no wooden door export business at all. In 1933, the year when the British empire trade agreements were negotiated, we exported 50,000 doors, and that number increased to about
1.000.	000 doors in 1938. In looking over the figures I found that our exports went to 1,681,000 doors in 1936, when business was a little better, or nearly 2,000,000 doors in that year, and then with the drop in business generally the figure came down to about
1.000.	000 doors in 1938. The development of the door industry, particularly in British Columbia, has been almost spectacular since 1933. Many United States firms have been forced to open up factories in Canada, and subsidiary industries such as the plywood industry, have been established. Under the British empire trade agreements we enjoyed a preference of two shillings and sixpence on doors, whereas under this treaty the duty is one shilling and sixpence, and this gentleman told me-and what he said has been confirmed

by others-that as a result of the cutting down of our preference of two shillings and sixpence to one shilling and sixpence, the door industry in British Columbia is going to be completely wiped out. They say that this difference is just sufficient to drive the business to the western states; to Tacoma, the hon. member for Kootenay East suggests. This gentleman told me that in two more years there will be no more door industry in British Columbia.
Take coal. The dominion bureau of statistics reports that our Canadian production of coal last year amounted to 14.000,000 tons, and 15,800,000 tons in 1937. Our imports amounted to 13,500,000 tons, or just about the same as our Canadian production. These figures should be read in the light of the declaration that was made in the Nova Scotia brief presented to the dominion government last week, wherein it was asserted that the present Canadian duty on coal is wholly inadequate, and the fact that it has been further reduced by the elimination of the excise tax makes a difference, if I remember the calculation rightly, of seventeen cents a ton .in the duty. My hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) shakes his head.

I should like to deal briefly with one or two quotas, and I am very glad to say that I am getting near the end of my remarks. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister said that I used unfairly the words " propaganda or ballyhoo " in a discussion of the quotas under this treaty. I said, Mr. Speaker, that in the press release which was issued respecting the treaty, these quotas were made to appear enormous, whereas many of them are absolutely laughable, and some of the statements are deceitful.
Let me deal briefly with the milk quota. I do not pretend to be an authority on agriculture, but I am giving these facts, and I have no doubt they are absolutely accurate.

While our milk quota by this treaty is 3,000,000 gallons, Canadian production last year amounted to 1,700,000,000 gallons.
Mr. DUNNING We drink a great deal of our production.

Of course, but a quota of only 3,000,000 gallons out of a production of
1,700,000,000 gallons shows the picayune size of the quota on milk. It is just a joke.
I saw an item in the press the other day-and I have it here-showing that the milk sold in Ottawa last year amounted to over 4,000,000 gallons, and yet our quota, of which this government boasts so loudly, is only 3,000,000 gallons. My secretary, who has a mathematical turn of mind, figured it out this way, that if you take those 3,000,000 gallons and divide them among the people of the United States it means that each citizen of the United States would get one-fifth of a pint once a year. That is the quota of which hon. gentlemen opposite are boasting, and this, with the free market for vegetable oils, is severely injuring the dairy industry.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

Quite correct. I just
mentioned that it is hurting the dairy industry very much. I was not speaking of vegetable oils as being in the treaty. But milk is in the treaty. The quota on milk is a speck; it is not important, just a microscopic amount.
As regards potatoes, Canada's total production of potatoes in 1938 was 60,000,000 bushels, and that of the United States, 369,000,000 bushels, or a total of 429,000,000 bushels. Our quota into the United States is two and a half million bushels, and I am informed- and my statement has been confirmed by many who come from that section-that one county in New Brunswick could more than supply that quota. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has raised a good deal of wheat, but I did not think that he raised potatoes. He may eat them, like a good Irishman does.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Just now I represent potato growers, and they are very well pleased with the quota.

As I have said, our potatoes go into the United States under much greater restrictions, in addition to the limited quota, than those on United States potatoes coming into Canada. I ask myself, why the difference?
I wish now to deal with the cattle quota. This is a more important matter, because I maintain that the statement about the cattle quota as given to this house and to the people of this country in the press release was a deception-intentionally or accidentally, I am curious to know- I should like to know whether the government knew, when they got the quota of 225,000 cattle and advertised that in their press release, that it included! Mexico.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: We in the west knew it.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Why did they not mention it in the press release?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I think that inside three years the hon. gentleman and his party ought to have learned enough to tell the truth when they issue a press release. I am going to quote it. A copy of the press release issued by hon. gentlemen opposite is here, and this is what it says on pages 14 and 15 about the cattle quota:
For the prairie provinces the most important concession-
They are boasting of what they are doing for the country.
-in the trade agreement is the maximum reduction in the United States duty on heavy cattle and the enlargement of the tariff quota on this type of cattle considerably beyond that granted in the 1935 trade agreement.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

The most important of the agricultural concessions are those relating to live cattle. Western Canada is particularly interested in the United States duty on heavy cattle weighing 700 pounds or more each. On this type of cattle Canada is to receive the maximum reduction in duty or a rate of U cents per pound

Then he explains why they shut it off at the 55,000. In other words, of this supposed quota for the Canadian cattle raiser, the Mexican gets 45 per cent. That may please the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross); he seems to be quite tickled to death with it.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
But I do not think it
satisfies the western cattle raiser who was told he could ship in 60,000 cattle in that time.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: No, he was not.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: He was told it in the press release. Why deny it?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: No, he was not.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: There was no word said of Mexico.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It was in the last treaty, and this quota was increased by 70,000.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I do not suppose the cattle raiser read the terms of this treaty any more than he read the last one. This, I am told.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
is the first time it was ever mentioned in the parliament of Canada. A little further down the Minister of Agriculture said:
The quota will divide somewhat in the proportions of fifty-five per cent and forty-five per cent.
A little further down the hon. member for Haldimand asked:
Was it the intention that Canada should enjoy the whole 60,000 per quarter, or otherwise?
Mr Gardiner: No. Under the old agreement, the one which existed before, provision was made, whereby the quota would be for all the cattle imported into the United States. In practice it worked out that the cattle came from Mexico and Canada, and exactly the same terms are in the present agreement.
I ask, why was that not stated in the press release? My hon. friends implied that I was not quite fair in using the word "ballyhoo" or "propaganda". Certainly they might have said that this -was a global quota in which Mexico could share. Canada cannot now ship any more into the United States until the end of March; the quota was exhausted in January, with the result pointed out to me in a letter from a cattle raiser from the west, who says:
Our cattle will rule $1 to $1.50 per hundred lower for the next six weeks than they were selling at one week ago, and I can assure you that the feeders of live stock across this country are really mad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: That shows the value of the treaty to the cattle raiser, does it not?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It shows what he can get as long as he can ship cattle under the quota, but it does not show how long he can get them in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: As a matter of fact, many cattle were saved up for the coming info operation of the treaty.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Where was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: In Mexico, and here too, for that matter.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That may be; but I find
that last year, when Mexico was not saving up, they supplied 31-3 per cent of the cattle shipped into the United States. That was pretty nearly as high as this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Not of the class covered by this item.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Yes, exactly of the class. I have the figures here in a publication put out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce
(Mr. Euler), and I have a page torn from that publication, the Canadian Intelligence Journal.
Total exports of cattle weighing 700 pounds or more amounted during the calendar year to 124,903 head, or 80-2 per cent of the total quota. Of this total, 48,496 head or 31*3 per cent of the quota were shipped from Mexico.
Again I ask, why, in fairness to our people, was not Mexico mentioned? That is the only attitude I take in this connection, and it is a perfectly fair attitude.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It is a weak case for deception.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: My hon. friend may think so. His idea of deception and mine may be different. I do not know.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Apparently the
Minister of Trade and Commerce did not try to deceive them.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The hon. member is implying that the Minister of Finance did, because he denied it until I put up the Minister of Trade and Commerce against him.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
He put it out
last year.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That is all about that.
I do not wish to get into any wrangles; I am simply pointing out the facts. Let me read what they say in the United States press release with regard to cattle. It shows that they were not blind. At page 47 they say:
In making concessions to Canada on farm products, care has been taken to avoid the possibility of material hardship to any important group of producers in the United States. . . . The most important concessions to Canada in the live stock field are safeguarded by tariff quotas.
They knew what they were doing. This is just another illustration of the way in which they put it over. Now let me read a few more items from this press release, having no particular bearing on cattle but of interest for other reasons. For example, on page 1:
A major new concession to the United States results from the provision that hereafter the Canadian special import tax of 3 per cent will be removed from all items, dutiable or free, listed specifically in schedule 1 which names concessions by Canada.
Then on the next page:
On the other hand, the bulk of Canadian imports from the United States consists of dutiable commodities; consequently the commodities on which Canada has reduced its duties, make up a substantially larger value of trade than dp the commodities on which the United States lowered its duties.
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

Then on page 5:
Every section of the United States will benefit from the wide-reaching concessions made by Canada in the new trade agreement.
On page 9:
Under the trade agreements act the United States may not reduce any duty through a trade agreement by more than 50 per cent; but the Canadian government is under no such limitation, and, in some cases, the rates in schedule 1 are more than 50 per cent lower than those in effect in 1935, and some former duties have been removed altogether.
There are a good many more statements to the same effect, all showing clearly that we got the worst of it. They are so bad that I do not like to read them. On page 10 there is this statement:
By far the most important of the "bindings" of the rates of duty already in effect in 1935 relate to coal and coke, the imports of which from the United States to Canada in 1937 were valued at over $30,000,000. . . . The listing of these items in schedule 1 carries with it the removal of the 3 per cent excise tax, which in the case of many of the items on which the duties proper are low, constitutes a material fraction of the charges payable on importation into Canada. In the case of anthracite coal, the duty on which, bound by the agreement against increase, is 50 cents per ton (about 10 per cent in ad valorem equivalent), the tax is equal to about 17 cents per ton.
On the same page:
The new agreement provides that, in the case of all articles, dutiable or free, listed in schedule 1, the Canadian special excise tax of 3 per cent will be removed on imports from the_ United States as soon as the necessary legislation can be enacted. Since schedule 1 covers 57 per cent of the total of 1937 imports from this country, this provision means a large reduction in the charges heretofore collected.
On page 13:
Of the nine tariff quotas fixed in the new agreement, on dutiable and free items together, six are at figures which represent a very small percentage of our consumption. The limits on filleted fish, shingles, and nepheline syenite are relatively higher but are not high enough to permit serious injury to domestic producers should the tariff quotas be filled.
These quotations show how well they took care of their own people, and I commend them for having done so. They were right in safeguarding the interests of their own people and we should have done likewise. In regard to fruits and vegetables they say, on page 19:
The 1937 imports of United States fresh fruits and vegetables into Canada were valued at nearly $17,000,000. The new agreement provides for reductions in Canadian duties and other import charges on $14,500,000 worth of that trade, or 80 per cent of the total value of all agricultural items on which reduced duties result from the new agreement . . . These concessions represent benefits to fruit and vegetable growers and shippers in all parts of the United States.

In regard to apples:
This reduction on apples results from the fact that Canada has agreed to a substantial reduction in the margin of duty preference enjoyed by Canadian apples in the British market, an action of outstanding value to American apple growers and shippers.
Then on page 20: [DOT]
Duty reductions:-The new agreement establishes a basic duty of 10 per cent for nearly all of the fresh fruits and vegetables now subject to an ad valorem duty. Under the 1936 agreement the same items paid 15 per cent. Prior to 1936, the fruit items now dutiable at 10 per cent paid 20 per cent, while the vegetables were charged 30 per cent.
Here is another, on page 25, with reference to pulp, paper and printed matter:
A major concession of the 1936 agreement, continued in the new agreement, related to magazines and periodical publications. . . . Imports under periodicals of all kinds, including newspapers from the United States increased from $2,600,000 in 1935 to $5,900,000 in 1937, the gain being chiefly in the class from which the duties had been removed. The wider circulation of American magazines in Canada creates and stimulates demand for new and improved products and thereby benefits both Canadian and American manufacturers of such products.
Incidentally, it stimulates in Canada the purchase of many pulp magazines, some of which we would be far better without. On page 43 there is the following:
An important concession is made on boots and shoes. The 40 per cent rate of 1935 became 35 per cent in 1936 through the mostfavoured-nation provision. Imports increased from $343,000 in 1935 to $515,000 in 1937. The rate is now made 30 per cent by schedule 1, which is the same rate as applied in 1929 when imports from the United States were valued at over $2,000,000. *
On page 47:
The trade agreement with the United Kingdom. made at the same time as that with Canada, contains many concessions of benefit to American agriculture. Several of the concessions thus obtained involve the relinquishment, in whole or in part, of tariff preferences which Canada had previously held in the British market . . .
In making concessions to Canada on farm products, care has been taken to avoid the possibility of material hardship to any important group of producers in the United States.
On page 49:
Canada has now agreed to permit free entry of potatoes except during the 6-week period June 15 to July 31. at which time the duty will be half the former rate.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: What is the hon. member reading from?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: From the United States press release.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Propaganda like ours?

Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The hon. gentleman admits that theirs is propaganda. He contradicts his leader. I do not blame his leader for looking crossly at him at the moment.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I merely used the hon. gentleman's extravagant language. That is all.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The minister need not use any extravagant language of mine; he can be extravagant himself. This release was put out by the Department of State in Washington under the title, "The New Trade Agreement with Canada, signed November 17, 1938." It is an official document.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Does the hon. member consider that ballyhoo?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is ballyhoo, but I do know that a good deal of what my hon. friends put out was ballyhoo. In regard to the most favoured nation clause, I find that despite the fact that we get no concession from any of the favoured nations including Japan, Italy and Germany, we give them the same concessions as we give the United States. Here is Japan with a lower standard of living, very much lower than ours, with low wages, in some cases one-tenj.h of ours, in some cases one-fifth, with sweatshop conditions, no liberty to labour-and that applies to Germany and Italy-no labour unions, no right to bargain; and yet they are given the same rights as the United States under the favoured nation clause. How can Canada compete with such conditions? On another occasion I placed on record the wages paid in the textile industry of Japan, which are just one-tenth the wages paid textile employees in Canada. This provision will curtail the work and wages available in Canada, where the wages are equal to any in the world. Our duty on cotton goods, for example, is 161 per cent, while the British duty on similar goods is 22$ per cent. At the same time our wages are 60 per cent higher than the British wages. I am informed that our cotton industry is about 19 per cent below what it was in 1937.
The right hon. gentleman said what has been stated over and over again, and I suppose will be stated many times in future, that Great Britain asked for special concessions on the part of Canada in regard to the preferences, which would give an advantage to the United States. I asked that those letters be tabled, but the right hon. gentleman said they were too confidential. I want to protest again against this "too confidential" statement that is being made continually by hon. gentlemen opposite. If the right hon. gentleman has a right to quote from that correspondence, 714S2-68
this whole house has a right to read it. It is claimed that this agreement brings some advantage to the man on the street. That is questionable; instead of an advantage to the man on the street, what we get is more competition, less production and higher costs. That often happens when you lower tariffs; you have fewer jobs and less money with which to purchase the goods produced.
Then, with regard to the 3 per cent special excise tax, I assume this change will result in a great decrease in revenue. Last year I believe that tax brought in between fifteen and eighteen million dollars. I submit that the removal of the 3 per cent special excise tax on the items specified in the agreement was either bad faith or bad management on the part of the government. No announcement was made in connection with the matter until some days later, after protests began to reach the Minister of Finance because so many inequalities would result. Then the minister said that these would be corrected, but they have not been corrected yet. Here is the situation to-day, on account of the fact that the 3 per cent special excise tax has been removed only from the items mentioned in the schedule. Mushrooms and cut flowers are freed from the 3 per cent tax, but it remains on most of the necessities of life. The tax has been removed from such items as sweet potatoes, artichokes, asparagus, strawberries, quinces and nectarines, perfumery and alligator pears, but it remains on many raw materials and on clothing.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The excise tax is not off yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It has not been removed from any item yet.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I admit that; but the
government agreed to take it off, and I am sure my hon. friend would not contradict the statement that the government does intend to take it off. The situation to-day is that the go'-ernment has promised to remove the tax from the luxuries I have mentioned, these absolute unnecessaries, if I may coin a word, while they have said nothing about removing it from many raw materials and many kinds of clothing. To show the incongruity of this agreement, the excise tax is to be removed from raw cotton but it is to remain on raw wool and raw silk. It is to be removed from coal but will remain on certain types of coke.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Who says it will remain?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I say, according to the
agreement it will remain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Nothing of the kind.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The agreement distinctly
states that the 3 per cent excise tax is to be taken off the items covered by the agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Yes, but it does not say it will remain on anything else.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
No, and that is exactly
what I was going to say. Before the government has finished it will have to remove the tax from all items. The other day when the hon. member for Kootenay East pointed that out, the Minister of Finance shook his head, but I repeat that before we have finished we shall have to remove the special excise tax entirely. It must be done in order to remove the inequalities, absurdities and discriminations in the application of our duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Not because we have to; whatever we do will be in the interests of the Canadian people.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The hon. gentleman would not suggest that they would remove that tax from many of these unnecessaries, as I termed them a few moments ago, and leave it on the raw materials and necessities of life.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I take it that we would have my hon. friend's support in removing it?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
As long as the agreement is as it is, certainly you would have to have my support, because I would not want the country to get in the muddle it would be in if the situation remained as it would be without further removal of the 3 per cent tax. But the hon. gentleman and his government did not mention that in their press release. They simply stated that these were the reductions. It was only a few days later that this situation was pointed out to the Minister of Finance by many people who were vitally affected by it, people who would suffer from injustice if some remedy were not found. Then, a few days later, the hon. gentleman said:
The government will make certain when the necessary legislation is introduced that it will be of such a character as to eliminate any unfairness that might otherwise be expected to result from the exemption from the tax of the particular articles enumerated in the agreement.
With that I heartily agree. Otherwise the country would be left in a hopeless muddle. The situation could not possibly remain as it would be left under this agreement. There is no doubt, I further suggest, that this extension of the removal of the excise tax was not contemplated at the time the agreement was negotiated, so these are really new concessions to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Then why was it not mentioned among all the ballyhoo in the press release? Was it again deception?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, I will tell him.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can make his own speech when he wishes to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Very well.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: However, I do not mind interruptions. Tell me; why was it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The answer is this. We were making an agreement with the United States with respect to a specified list of commodities. Anything we do with respect to taxation outside the list of commodities under discussion is purely a matter of domestic policy for this parliament and not a matter for the United States.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I quite agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: That is why it was not mentioned.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: But since the minister was going to make a statement a few days later, why did not the government, in the press release, say that within a short time there would have to be other modifications in order to put the agreement on a fair basis?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: They were only announcing accomplished things.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
No; they were announcing a good many things which were not accomplished at all. To my mind this is simply another case of ministerial blundering.
In conclusion, let me repeat that at present it is impossible to state what will be the result of this treaty. Time alone will tell, but my belief is that the ill effects will be very much greater than the good effects. In 1935 this government made an agreement with the United States. In 1934, the year previous, our trade with the United States showed a balance in our favour of $1,000,000.' Last year our trade with the United States showed an unfavourable balance of $82,000,000; in other words, they sold us $82,000,000 worth of goods more than we sold them. Then it is interesting to note the increase of trade under the items covered by the 1935 agreement. Our exports under the items affected by the 1935 treaty increased by only $16,000,000; of that amount newsprint accounted for $15,000,000, and newsprint has been on the free list since 1913. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about their press release being so honest. Let me quote

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
what is said at page 26 of that press release, because this is the sort of half truth with which this release is filled:
In the 1935 trade agreement provision was made for the binding of the free entry of those kinds of wood pulp of which Canada was the chief supplier of imports into the United States. In the new trade agreement the binding of free entry is broadened to cover all kinds of mechanical and chemical wood pulps shipped from Canada to the United States. The free entry of standard newsprint paper is rebound in the new trade agreement and this covers the largest single item of trade between the two countries.
What is the implication there? It is that they got some great favour for Canada, when as a matter of fact all these things fiave entered the United States free, at least since 1913. If that is not propaganda; if that is not a half truth, I do not know one when I see it.
This agreement will help here and hurt there. The future will tell the result so far as Canada as a whole is concerned. My belief is, of course, that there is some good in this treaty. It would be a queer treaty if there were not some good items in it, though frankly I have not heard about them, and I am hearing more and more every day about the ill effects on the various industries of Canada. My conviction is also that the balance is largely against us.
After all, we have to aid Canada as a whole. This country is a nation, not nine nations, and we must treat it as a nation. I pointed out that the empire trade agreements bound the empire together economically; this trade agreement pulls the empire apart. When the Republicans again go into office in the United States, the chances are that this agreement will be cancelled. Then we shall have a changing of our trade routes and we shall have lost our preference. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, who follows me in the debate, made the statement in the house the other day that we would get back our preference. The preference will have been wiped out. It will not come back. If the Republicans take office in 1940, then probably this treaty would be wiped out, because they are a high protectionist party. If they do, and if it is wiped out, does anybody suggest that we shall get back our preference?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I do not agree with the hon. member. He says we do.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It is in the agreement.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Yes, but it will be a fait accompli; we shall not get it back. There is certainly room for discussion, and we intend 71492-68J
to tell the people what has not been told by the government. We intend to tell the facts and the truth-what we should have in all government business.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I say at the outset that I realize my inability adequately to deal with some of the statements made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion). He has quite properly taken some two hours to deliver his address and to make his criticisms. I appreciate the fact that I am confined to forty minutes, and I believe it is quite impossible for me fully to deal with some of the statements he has made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: You cannot use a scrapbook in forty minutes.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: But you put out forty-two pages of propaganda, to begin with. You do not need as much time.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: But I should like to use as much of my forty minutes as possible.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

speechtext: I have just had brought to my attention a statement giving a comparison of figures with respect to exports to the United States.' Our exports to that country in the month of January, 1939, were valued at $36,276,766.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

While I am not an economist, and while I have every respect for the opinion of my hon. friend [DOT]opposite, I cannot see why, when gold is produced in Canada by the labour of our men, when it adds to the wealth of Canada and when it is exported as a commodity, it cannot fairly be included in the sum of our exports.

fMr. Euler.]

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
just as an indication to my learned friends that perhaps they need not fear what was so apparent in my hon. friend's speech, that this country was going to be ruined as a result of this trade agreement.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I am going to be rather discursive in my remarks, in touching upon some of the points mentioned by my hon. friend to-day. He spoke of the fact, and it is a fact, that on some commodities the Canadian duties are much lower than the duties on the same commodities going into the United States. I have not had an opportunity to look into this to any extent, but I might quote a few instances where the shoe is on the other foot.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I admit there are some.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: There are some commodities that go into the United States at lower rates than into Canada. Patent leather goes into the United States in fairly large volume and the duty imposed against it is 7i per cent. The Canadian duty on patent leather from the United States is 20 per cent. They have a duty against rubber tires of 10 per cent, whereas our duty against them is 25 per cent.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: As a matter of information, do any Canadian rubber tires go into the United States?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I do not think so, but the rate is there. They have a rate of 10 per cent against automobiles from Canada, whereas our rate is 174 per cent. Agricultural implements are admitted into the United States free, and some do go in, whereas we have a rate of 7i per cent. The rate on cereal breakfast foods entering the United States is 10 per cent, whereas the Canadian rates are from 15 to 25 per cent. The rate on whisky entering the United States is $2, whereas the Canadian rate is $6.
My hon. friend said something about press releases, indicating that the Canadian press release was pretty much propaganda for the government. Perhaps he made a point in connection with the cattle quota, but I think it might have been as well if it had been stated that, as in the previous agreement of 1934, the cattle quota is a world quota. The hon. member cited some figures to show that this quota was divided pretty well in the present quarter between Canada and Mexico. That is quite true because they are the only countries exporting cattle to the United States. He went on to show that the quota had been exhausted during the first quarter, and that
Mexico had received a large proportion of the quota. That is also perfectly true. I believe hon. members across the floor will appreciate my statement when I say that this situation has received the attention of the government. Without disclosing anything' that should not be disclosed, I think I can say that the cattle exporters of this country will be well satisfied when they know what action is to be taken with regard to the quota, on cattle going into the Lhiited States.
In regard to my hon. friend's reference to the Canadian press release as propaganda, I leave it to him to say whether it is not just as reasonable for me to assume that the press release which was sent out by this government was just as fair, just as accurate and just as representative of the real situation as was the press release in the United States, from which he quoted so freely.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
They certainly could not
both be right.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
They might both be right.
My hon. friend has read a good deal from his scrap-book, for which I do not blame him. Before I conclude my remarks, which will be brief, I may be obliged .to do the same thing in order to combat some of the statements which he has made. My hon. friend minimizes and deprecates the argument put forth by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that trade agreements between countries like Canada and the United States, and the United States and Great Britain, have an influence on the goodwill that ought to exist between countries. I do not believe my hon. friend is quite serious in what he says. The buying and selling of goods by individuals often result in personal friendships. I remember once being a delegate to the League of Nations, and I thought then, as I do now, that the greatest value of the league was in the delegates from the various countries coming together to sit round a table, getting to know each other and realizing they were all pretty much .the same in their outlook. If that is -true of individuals, is it not true of nations? We have absolute proof of that right here. In spite of the disapproval of the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George-and I shall take back my statement if he objects-never in the history of nations has the feeling between Great Britain and the United States and Canada been as friendly as it is to-day.
I should like to turn, during the .time I have at my disposal, to the more material side of the agreement rather than deal with what might be regarded as the sentimental side, of which I spoke just now. I would say that the first principle which we as a
Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement

government desired to observe in making an agreement with the United States-and 1 think they were actuated by the same principle-was that we should try to make an agreement which would be mutually advantageous. That is the only basis upon which a permanent agreement can be framed. I was surprised at the statement of my hon. friend that the United States always gets the best of us. I believe he said that he would be afraid to negotiate with them for fear they would always get the best of us.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
That sort of thing comes

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I did not say that.

speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I will give figures to show that it means that and nothing else. In the fiscal year 1938, our imports of shoes from the United States were 307,000 pairs, and the total consumption in Canada was 22,723,000 pairs. If you figure that out, our imports of shoes from the United States, if we disregard those brought over occasionally under the S100 exemption, amounted to less than one and a half per cent of our consumption. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that under those conditions we cannot regard the competition as particularly strong.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: We must have had a fairly good protective tariff.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It still is a good protective tariff, and that is one of the points I desire to make. But the argument of my hon. friend would mean that, in spite of the fact that imports of United States boots and shoes amount to only one and a half per cent of our total consumption in Canada, we ought to impose a duty that would shut out those imports altogether, and that he must be in favour of a prohibitive tariff.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION

The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said that they are only restored-

speechtext: In the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, speaking in the house on January 31, 1939, as reported on page 479 of Hansard, contended that the exclusion' of preferences from the scope of most favoured nation treatment in no sense affirms the right of Canada to grant such preferences and leaves the United States free to condemn such preferences on diplomatic grounds.	*

Article 17 of the trade agreement reads:
Nothing in the agreement-
I am saying that this in effect reaffirms that we have preferences in the United Kingdom market which will be restored to us:
Nothing in the agreement shall entitle the United States of America to claim the benefit of any treatment, preference or privilege which may now or hereafter be accorded by Canada exclusively to territories under the sovereignty

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
of His Majesty the King of Great Britain, Ireland and the British dominions beyond the seas, Emperor of India, or under his majesty's protection or suzerainty.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: As a matter of information, has that not been the rule right along for years? I understand that it has been.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It was not included in the agreement.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It never was necessary
because the agreement in other terms made it clear.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Is that arrangement
countervailing?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I do not think there is any countervailing arrangement.
In conclusion I should like to speak of some concessions which Canada obtained, but I can speak of them only in very general terms. The new agreement renews or betters all the concessions secured for Canadian exports under the 1935 agreement, and contains a large number of entirely new concessions. Whereas the 1935 agreement provided for reductions in United States duties affecting sixty-three items and sub-items of the United States tariff-and now I am using some of the arguments of my hon. friend; I am speaking of ''items," although I admit quite freely that the number of items has no real bearing on the matter; it is the amount of money involved ; you might have half a dozen small items which w'ould not counterbalance one large item-the new agreement includes 129 reductions in rates of duty covering trade valued in 1937 at 872,981,492. In addition, there are forty-one bindings of existing United States rates of duty, including thirty-two rates reduced in the 1935 agreement. The total trade affected by these bindings was valued in 1937 at $51,843,682. Furthermore, the 1935 agreement contained a number of quotas limiting the imports allowed at reduced1 rates of duty. In each case in which it was found that these quotas actually restricted Canadian exports, the new agreement provides for a complete removal of, or a substantial increase in, the quota.
Finally, existing free entry was bound on thirty-two items and subitems in the new agreement, compared with twenty in the 1935 agreement.
The following are some of the principal concessions to Canada in the new trade agreement:
Agricultural products: Maximum reduction in duty on an enlarged quota in the case of

Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement
heavy cattle; enlarged tariff quota for calves; maximum reductions in the duties on cream and milk; further reduction in duty on cheese -this is very important-further reduction in the duty on horses; reductions in the duties on oats, barley, rye, buckwheat and products made therefrom; reductions in the duties on various kinds of feeds, fresh and frozen blueberries, clover and grass seeds, certified seed and table potatoes, hay, maple sugar and maple syrup, and silver or black fox furs or skins.
Fishery products: Reductions in duty covering almost the entire range of production of fish.
Forest products: Removal of the requirement that imported lumber should be marked with country of origin; removal of tariff quota applicable to imports, at reduced rates of duty, of Douglas fir and western hemlock lumber; more favourable arrangement regarding imports of red cedar shingles; reduced duties on a variety of woodenware articles; and on uncoated printing paper, hanging paper, tissue papers and crepe paper.
Minerals and metals: Reduced duties on a large number of them. I will not enumerate them.
Chemicals: The same.
Manufactured goods: Binding of free entry for agricultural implements, and reduced duties on patent leather; horsehide and cowhide gloves; skating boots; pipe organs; yachts; hose; wire cloth; axles; iron castings; moulders' patterns; iron and steel chains; electric stoves and ranges; electric washing machines; and waste.
In addition to the benefits which will be derived by Canadian exporters from the reductions in United States duties provided for in the new Canada-United States trade agreement, there are a great many concessions in the trade agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States which will facilitate Canadian trade. I have already made mention of this. Some of these are: Books; abrasives; sole leather; side upper leather; collar, bag and case leathers; grained leather; boots and shoes; numerous textile items; dressed furs; kippered herring; biscuits; jellies, jams and marmalades; ginger ale, and so on.
I will conclude, since my hon. friend has read from so many authorities, with some of the opinions of the Canadian public, or Canadian journals, as to the probable effect of the trade agreement. These are not in general taken from the columns of papers which are friendly to this government.
I have here a telegram received from the president of the British Columbia Lumber and Shingle Association:
At a meeting of our directors to-day I was instructed to wire you expressing our appreciation and thanks for the efforts that you and your department put forward in the recent trade negotiations to protect the lumber interests of our country and to advise that we fully appreciate that you had a difficult task to handle, particularly affecting lumber. We fully realized from the start some sacrifice would have to be made in empire markets in the interest of broader trading and sounder national relations but we are hopeful that when the United States removes the present excise tax that we will be able to more than regain our losses. I should also like to express my personal sincere congratulations and thanks.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: 'Would the minister give the dates of these?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
This is November 23 of last year.
The Windsor Star of November 19 said that cash will flow, and that the treaty is important to Windsor because of the car industry, which can look foward to better times.
The Ottawa Journal says that praise for the new Canada-United States agreement was general with representatives of the majority of industries.
The Hamilton Spectator says that the spirit behind the agreement stamps it as a healthy symptom in world economy.
The Montreal Gazette states that while there may be some difference of opinion as to the merits of the agreement, it can be said that it is bound to have a stimulating effect on world trade.
The Toronto Star writes that the treaty should commend itself to Canadians of all parties.
The London Free Press remarks that on general principles the people will approve the new treaties on political as well as economic grounds.
The Farmers Advocate believes that wider markets are opened through the trade agreement with the United States.
The Winnipeg Free Press quotes J. A. McLeod, president of the Bank of Nova Scotia, that the new three-cornered agreement is a great achievement in reducing trade barriers.
Saturday Night predicts an increase in trade, which will add to Canadian national wealth, and better times.
The Winnipeg Free Press quotes Hon. Howard Ferguson as strongly approving the agreement.
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

The Montreal Herald says that the signing of the treaty is one of the most hopeful signs which has appeared on the world horizon for a long time.
The Monetary Times states that the new treaty will affect the volume of international trade.
The Canadian Textile Journal believes that the new trade agreement will lessen restrictions on international trading that should have a fav-reaehing effect.
The Canada Lumberman, the Montreal Gazette and again La Presse are all favourable. I might say for the benefit of my good friend the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) that far from the textile mills in Hespeler having been injured, they are busy in that town, and in Preston they have gone back from a three-day to a five-day week. In regard to live stock Mr. Wright of Saskatchewan states:
Lowered tariff of half-cent on live cattle increases the value of all Canadian cattle approximately $5 per head.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Is that Mr. Wright of
the Globe and Mail?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
No. This is a gentleman
from Saskatchewan who, I believe, was a member of the board of the Bank of Canada.
Now let me give a few comments from United States sources.
The Mining Congress Journal of the United. States states that the zinc mining industry has been sacrificed in the agreement and complains bitterly.
The Milwaukee Sentinel states that the dairymen attack the treaty, complaining of the reduction in American tariffs on cream, milk, cheese and other dairy products.
The Duluth Herald objects to provisions that lower the duties on dairy products from Canada.
The New York Journal American states that there is severe criticism of the agreement on the part of members of congress who come from industrial states.
Senator H. Shipstead of Minnesota asks, "if this is Yankee trading, or are we trading the Yankee?" He says that the treaty is based more on international politics than on economics.
The New York Times protests against the agreement.
The Boston Post says that the pact hurts New England, and is loud in protest on behalf of the fishing and textile industries of New England which it says are injured.

The New York Herald-Tribune regards the new trade pact as a blow to the United States fisheries.
The lumbermen, the sheep and cattle men complain. The cattle men declare that they are sold down the river.
The New York Journal American states that United States farmers are sold out.
I have cited these opinions to show that there are views on both sides, and I say to the leader of the opposition that we shall have to wait and see exactly what the results will be.
This agreement was conceived in the spirit of goodwill and mutual advantage. No one contends that it is perfect, and only time and experience will disclose definitely its advantages and disadvantages. We believe that it is action in the right direction and that its enactment will be to the advantage of both countries.

speechtext:
Mr. WILFRID LACROIX (Quebec-Mont-morency) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of the bill which I have the honour to introduce is to ensure that employees of certain public services in the province of Quebec have the necessary qualifications for their work. Inasmuch as the chief qualification required in any public service is the ability to speak the language of the people with whom one has to deal, the proposed amendment seeks to authorize the board of railway commissioners to make orders and regulations providing that all new employees of railways, telegraph and telephone companies in the province of Quebec be sufficiently conversant with the French language to be able properly to perform their duties and to be understood by and understand a majority of the people with whom they are called upon to do business.
The situation in that regard in the province of Quebec is deplorable. In spite of all the complaints lodged by the travelling public

and others using these services, and their requests for an improvement in the situation, there has been no improvement. Why? Because there has been no change in the custom of appointing to positions in these public utility companies men who are totally ignorant of the French language. Let me take as an example that part of the Canadian National system situated in the province of Quebec and administered from Moncton. Nearly one-third of this division is located within the province of Quebec, and a considerable part of the remainder is in a French-speaking section of New Brunswick. On that division the following new appointments were made during 1937: brakemen, fifteen, of whom only two can speak French; firemen (apprentices), thirty, of whom only three can speak French; shop apprentices, thirty-nine, all but three unable to speak French; headquarters and supervisory staff, six, none of whom can speak French; legal department, seven, all unable to speak French; assistant superintendent of pensions, two. both unable to speak French: staff of the general superintendent of transportation, nine, all unable to speak French; traffic department, twelve, only two of whom can speak French; electric power and signal department, seven, not one oS.. whom can speak French; purchasing department. four, all unable to speak French; engineering department, six, all unable to speak French; auditing department, ten, none of whom can speak French; telephone and telegraph department, three, all unable to speak French; divisional superintendent's office, twelve, not one of whom can speak French; Canadian National express, seven, all unable to speak French; freight claims department, three, only one of whom can speak French; treasurer's department, four, all unable to speak French; local freight agent's office, three, all unable to speak French; general baggage agent's office, three, all unable to speak French; and so on.
In the town of Shediac, New Brunswick, for instance, where the population is ninety per cent French-speaking, there are three officials of the Canadian National Railways: a station agent, his assistant and a porter, not one of whom can speak French. It is high time that we changed this state of affairs; the French-Canadians are sick and tired of it. Even in our good old city of Quebec the express agent bears the name Corrigan MacManus; the telegraph agent is a Mr. McWilliams; the superintendent of the St. Malo shops is a Mr. Boone; the superintendent of the Saguenay division is a Mr. Edgley; the head of the bridge department L a Mr. Riddock; the head of the sleeping car department is a Mr. McDougall; the head of the mechanical department is a Mr. Broad-hurst ; the superintendent of the transportation department is a Mr. Sunderland; the official in charge of steamships is a Mr. Trueman, and so it goes in a dozen other cases.
In this connection I cannot do better than quote the testimony of a former railway employee who is now a member of this house, the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Lapointe), who on June 22, 1938, said:
It is clear that there exists within the Canadian National Railways an organization which is seeking to eliminate French-Canadians from the posts to which they are entitled. I therefore consider it necessary to investigate this situation, which should not be allowed to continue. Our English speaking friends may be tired of hearing our often repeated complaints, but I wish to tell them that, if we were used a little more fairly, if we were not always kept in the background, we would not so often deem it our painful duty to discuss with such frequency a problem very disagreeable to us.
In order to show them the actual situation, I invite them to visit w'ith me the province of Quebec where we will effect a little investigation. Let us first go to Montreal, and visit the shops or the large offices of the Canadian National Railways on McGill street.
If my hon. friends pay a visit to the different branches-traffic, finance, accounting, purchasing, industry, natural resources, etc.,- they will not find more than two French-Canadians out of every twenty employees. They will also find that French Canadians have been almost ostracized from important positions and that high salaries never go to them. They will look in vain for bilingual signs, either on the walls or on the office doors. If they ask the elevator operator for information in French, they probably will receive the same answer as I got, a few weeks ago: "I do not understand. All that is going on in the greatest French centre of America.
I will then ask my hon. friends to travel to the eastern part of the province of Quebec. But, before we leave Bonaventure station, we will pay a short visit to the offices of the sleeping car department. My hon. friends will no doubt be received as I was a few days ago when I spoke French to one of the employees: "Do you speak English?" said he. "If so. all right, because nobody here understands French."
We will then board the Ocean Limited, the night express, where further surprises await my hon. friends. In the sleeping cars, they will try in vain to make themselves understood in the French language. After a night's rest, we will go to the dining car. In any of the places between Rimouski and Matapedia, the stretch covered from 6 to 9 a.m., when the train passes through one of -the most beautiful districts of the province of Quebec, which is also one of the most exclusively French, I defy them to find among the eight members of the staff of that car a single one who can speak French.
