Yes. It was reintroduced last year as Bill No. 4. It was again opposed by the government, but entirely on constitutional grounds. The labourers' right to organize was apparently conceded by everyone-at least no one objected. But the British North America Act was invoked once more and we heard a good deal about property and civil rights.
The minister will recognize that I am a mere layman, but in my own way I tried to present certain constitutional arguments. I should like very briefly to run over the ground I took last year. I had been looking over the criminal code, and I brought to the
attention of the house certain sections of that code. I found, for example, that breach of trust by a public officer is a crime punishable by five years imprisonment. I found that obstructing an officiating clergyman is a crime for which one is liable to be sentenced to two years in prison. This does not mean that religion comes under federal jurisdiction, but when someone attempts to obstruct an officiating clergyman the act becomes a crime. I found, further, that the head of a family is required to provide the necessities of life for any child under sixteen and for his wife, and if he fails he is guilty of a crime and liable to a penalty of $500 or one year's imprisonment or both. Again I would say that this is not because family matters are matters that come under the jurisdiction of this parliament, but when someone evades certain responsibilities it becomes a crime. I find that the issuing of a false prospectus, statement or account by directors or officers of a company is a crime. Here again is a matter that is concerned with contracts, which come directly under provincial jurisdiction; yet if there is a false prospectus issued oi anything of that kind-though, and indeed because-affecting property and civil rights that becomes a crime. I found that ever cheating in playing at any game or in holding the stakes or in betting on any event is a crime rendering one liable to three years' imprisonment. I found that sending a false telegram is a crime, the punishment being two years imprisonment. I should like to read section 501 of the criminal code:
Everyone is guilty of an offence punishable, at the option of the accused, on indictment or on summary conviction before two justices and liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $100, or to three months' imprisonment with or without hard labour, who wrongfully and without lawful authority, with a view to compel any other person to abstain from doing anything which he has a lawful right to do, or to do anything from which he has a lawful right to abstain . . .
I submit that clause is closely in line with the bill which I present to-night.
Let us take another section, section 502:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who, in pursuance of any unlawful combination or conspiracy to raise the rate of -wages . . . uses any violence or threat of violence to any person, with intent to hinder him from working or being employed at such trade, business or manufacture.
Here is a matter that on the face of it might be considered a purely provincial matter, having to do with contracts, wages, et cetera; but when anyone undertakes to prevent an employee from doing work under

these circumstances, his action is a crime and comes under the jurisdiction of this parliament. As I pointed out last year, certain things which employees may do become crimes. And I suggest that if we have a provision against such actions we should also have in the criminal code a provision preventing employers from interfering with employees in their efforts to organize or carry on union activities. It seems to me that is a reasonable provision.
I am not a lawyer. But I remember nearly forty years ago having to coach a few law students in logic. I must say that after the experience of those weeks I have never been overwhelmed by what the lawyers instinctively know about reasoning or accept unreservedly their conclusions.

But I submit there is no inherent quality in a lawyer as such which makes his deductions necessarily logical.
With regard to the -constitutional aspects of the case I should like to quote from the submission made by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations in January of last year. Referring to the jurisdictional question the submission states:
We base this statement on two important principles laid down by the privy council itself in dealing with our constitution. The first of these principles was given in a decision of 1896 (the Distillers' and Brewers' case), when their lordships stated that they did not doubt "that some matters, in their origin local and provincial, might attain such dimensions as to affect the body politic of the dominion and to justify the Canadian parliament in passing laws for their regulation or abolition in the interests of the dominion." Obviously this means that a matter of civil rights or of a local or private nature in its origin should cease to be reserved exclusively to the provinces when it becomes of such prominence as to attain national significance.
The second principle, contained in the decision on the Radio case (1932) may be taken either as an extension of the first, or as parallel to it. Lord Dunedin in giving judgment had established that the point at issue was given by the act neither to the dominion nor to the provinces. As a residual power, and as a matter essentially national, jurisdiction was declared to rest with the federal authority.
One other paragraph of this document.
Thus, it seemed to the trades and labour congress that the intention in the mind of the original promoters of the British North America Act and the needs of to-day in regard to the constitution are in agreement, namely, that the central government should be able to exercise those functions one "would expect to find a

central government possessing, that is to say, jurisdiction in questions of common import throughout the nation in matters where uniformity is highly desirable, in matters where the size of the problem exceeds provincial competence, as well as in matters more readily recognized as interprovineial in scope.
Later in the debate last year I was very glad to have the hearty support of the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Bennett. As we all recognize him as a lawyer of standing, I take the liberty of quoting a few paragraphs which I think fairly well summarize his argument. This is to be found on pages 3994, 3995 and 3996 of Hansard for 1938:
I think the right hon. Minister of Justice will agree with me that in two paragraphs of this bill we are not dealing with property and civil rights at all, that what we are dealing with is intimidation and conspiracy.
I hope the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will take this point very carefully into consideration, "what we are dealing with is intimidation and conspiracy." The quotation continues:
In the paragraph to which I refer, paragraph (b), we are dealing with the offence against the body politic on the part of those who may be in a position to enforce their views by threats, intimidation or otherwise, preventing that which arises out of property and civil rights, namely a contract being made effective. No one would question the right of the provinces to control matters of property and civil rights. No one has questioned the right of the provinces to deal with matters of contract. But it does not follow that because that is so, this parliament in the exercise of its jurisdiction over criminal law may not express itself in the strongest possible terms as to those who interfere with freedom of contract and the making of it. . . .
Again:
But where a man says, " 'Thou shalt not' use your property or exercise your civil rights," and he uses towards you intimidation or force or threats to see that you do not exercise your rights, that is an offence; that is within the criminal law, and solely within the jurisdiction of this parliament. It is that offence at which this bill strikes.
And again, with respect to penalties:
But it is not a penalty for a breach of contract, because that is covered by a provincial statute; that penalty sounds in damages, as many acts provide. This bill goes further. It does not, as I read it, contemplate the question of contract or property and civil rights in that sense at all. It merely says that if a man refuses to employ another, or dismisses him from his employment because he has exercised his freedom of choice by associating himself with a particular trade union, that is such a deprivation of a civil right, the great right of freedom or association, as to incur the penalties of the criminal law, and not a pecuniary result sounding in damages. That, I think, is the distinction between the provincial statutes and this bill.

The then leader of the opposition offered a practical suggestion:
On the other hand, if we have what I conceive to be the strongest reason in the world for believing a statute to be valid, we should place it on the statute books and ask that it be referred to the court so that its validity may be determined. That is the method prescribed by law for that purpose.
He considered that under these circumstances the bill need not be proclaimed. He closed his presentation with this statement:
I believe the bill to be valid. I believe it to be within the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament. I believe it makes it an adequate and proper offence for a person to interfere with any man exercising his freedom of choice and his right of association, provided always that it is exercised-in the language of the bill itself-"in a lawful manner."
The United States, I might point out, has had somewhat similar constitutional difficulties. The National Labour Relations Act of 1938, though challenged in the courts, was upheld by the supreme court. The core of the National Labour Relations Act lies in sections 7 and 8. Section 7 provides:
Employees shall have the right to selforganization, to form, join, or assist labour organization, to bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing, and to engage in concerted activities, for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection.
Section 8 supplements and enforces the right of employees to organize and bargain collectively by enumerating and prohibiting certain practices by employers, which are designated as "unfair labour practices." And I would call these particular sections to the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers):
1.	It is declared to be an unfair labour practice for an employer to "interfere with, restrain or coerce employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in section 7."
2.	It is an unfair labour practice " to dominate or interfere with the formation or administration of a labour organization or contribute financial or other support to it."
3.	It is an unfair labour practice for an employer "by discrimination in regard to hire or tenure of employment or any term or condition of employment to encourage or discourage membership in any labour organization."
4.	An employer indulges in an unfair labour practice if he discharges or discriminates against an employee because he has filed charges against an employer under the act.
5.	An employer indulges in an unfair labour practice when he refuses to bargain collectively with the representatives of his employees.
Let me reiterate that this measure, whose constitutionality was challenged, was sustained in the United States by the supreme court.
We are urging this bill at this time because in practice it has been found that the provincial legislation is wholly inadequate. Had I time I might review the provincial acts in the various provinces, but I do not think that is necessary here to-night. I should like to confine myself to the objection raised last year, the constitutional objection.

Since this matter was last discussed in the House of Commons I have had some experience in industrial strife which has led me to the firm conviction that only a measure of this kind will guarantee to the workers of Canada their fundamental rights-freedom of association and equality before the law. I propose to tell a plain, unvarnished tale of events which occurred in British Columbia last summer and which demonstrated how men may be deprived of these fundamental civil rights by powerful, vested interests. In this instance something like thirty-one men were convicted before our courts as a result of their struggle to assert their rights. I refer to the strike that took place at Blubber Bay, Texada island.
Quariying operations on Texada island are conducted by the Pacific Lime Company. Texada is an isolated spot and the company controls virtually the only payroll on the island. They enjoy practically a monopoly of the source of first-class lime on the Pacific coast, both on the Canadian and on the United States side, and usually they employ about 150 men. I have no hesitation in saying on my responsibility as a member, and after careful investigation of the conditions there, that this particular company has a most unsavoury record at the coast so far as working conditions are concerned. It is a notorious fact that they have failed to enforce the usual safety regulations in the mill, in the quarry and in connection with ventilation in the sacking room. On one occasion, a man, because a shaft was unguarded, was caught, and before the accident was discovered about twenty minutes later, he was mincemeat. Mr. Justice McIntosh, who presided on the arbitration board, found it necessary to recommend that rubble round the lip of the pit should be cleared away. When men are working in a quarry 189 feet deep, from which the only egress is a straight, narrow ladder, it is obvious that a stone, falling from that height, might easily crush a man's skull. Other industrialists on the coast have felt quite uneasy for many years about the conditions that obtained at Blubber Bay. The wage arrangements were also unsatisfactory. The men attempted to organize, and in consequence of that attempt their leaders were definitely blacklisted by the company. During the summer of 1937, and again in the summer of 1938, they insisted on their rights of collective bargaining and of organization. They took all the legal processes available to them under the laws of British Columbia. Conciliators were sent in on three

occasions and, conciliation having failed, the men took action under which is known as the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act of British Columbia. Mr. Justice McIntosh presided over the board of arbitration, and the board brought down a unanimous finding on the main points submitted to them. The provincial act provides:
It shall be lawful for employees to bargain collectively with their employers, and to conduct such bargaining through representatives of employees duly elected by a majority vote of employees affected, and any employer or_ employees refusing so to bargain shall be liable to a fine not exceeding $500 for each offence.
The board found in favour of the men on all the principal points under dispute, and the award was unanimous. The company accepted the award. True, there were some technical difficulties at the time, but Mr. Justice McIntosh, accompanied by several members of the board, went back to Blubber Bay and ironed out these difficulties. Again, the award was accepted by all parties to the dispute. Mr. Justice McIntosh recommended that the twenty-three men previously blacklisted should be reinstated. His position was made quite clear in that respect. He said that the company should dismiss the men who had been temporarily employed during the course of the dispute and that those who had been dismissed should be reinstated if available. Nevertheless this company, almost wholly owned and controlled entirely by a United States concern, the Niagara Alkali Company, New York, although accepting the award, refused to work out conditions of reinstatement for the men concerned. The men waited between two and three weeks patiently expecting the company to devise a plan of reinstatement, but still the company refused to reemploy them. The men went on strike and from then on we had one of the most tragic series of incidents in British Columbia, constituting a dark blot on the industrial history of that province; for not only was it shown that the provincial legislation was inadequate, that it was impossible for the provincial government to enforce the award, but the company figuratively thumbed its nose at the law; and what made it still worse, the detachment of provincial police sent to Blubber Bay was employed to suppress the strikers.
The company, through the cooperation of the police, enforced their owm padlock law on Texada island. Families residing on private property and desiring to cross on the only thoroughfare available in order to get to the only store, the only telephone and telegraph office, the government dock and the public highway, were compelled to secure passes from

the company's office, and on one occasion, in order to reach the public highway from private property, I was required, though a member of this house on lawful business, to travel under police escort. It was a terrible situation and one w'hich has led to extreme bitterness in British Columbia. That strike is still pending. The result was to make a travesty of law and justice in that province, and after what has occurred at Blubber Bay, and in view of the circumstances that surrounded that strike, it is no wonder that many people have little confidence in the administration of law and order in our country. It is nine o'clock now and I desire to move the adjournment of the debate.	.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for approval of the trade agreement between Canada and the United States, entered into at Washington on November 17, 1938, subject to required legislation.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
In
rising to speak on the trade treaty I find myself in a most difficult position. I could praise this treaty with justice perhaps, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) have done, and in so doing unquestionably win the applause and approval of the Liberals in the house and their supporters outside. On the other hand I could disparage the treaty with equal show of reason, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has abundantly demonstrated, and in so doing I should win the approbation of the Conservatives in the house and their supporters outside.
But I am here to preach a new doctrine, a doctrine of understanding. It is my task to point a new way. If I understand; if I have a new way, I shall stand alone; for it is well known that he who understands, stands alone. I believe there is a way out of the difficulties by which we are beset, and as long as I have that faith I shall endeavour to find that way and to assist my fellow Canadians in finding it, even if in so doing I must, to a great extent, stand alone. Consequently I will not approve this treaty, nor will I condemn it. In my opinion the good points offset the bad ones, and there are in the treaty a sufficiently large number of both.
It would appear as though in the last analysis it might favour the west in considerable

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
measure. It would seem that it might assist my province and my constituency, at least *directly; whether or not it will assist indirectly it is too early to say. Consequently I will watch the treaty and the way it works out, with much interest.
Before going further, I am going to lay down this general principle, which I was pleased to hear the leader of the opposition lay down. Before any change is brought about in the tariff structure of Canada, by any administration whatever, all producers whose interests may be affected directly or indirectly by any such change ought to be given full right and opportunity to come before the people concerned in making the change and to present their case, in whatever detail they consider necessary, in order to make everyone fully understand their point *of view.
There is a tendency on the part of the leader of the government, the right hon. Prime Minister, to try to misrepresent just a little the stand of the people who oppose him in this country. If one says the least word against trade, or even damns it with faint praise, immediately the leader of the government rises in his place and seeks to take advantage and make political capital of the situation by trying to make it appear that such person opposes trade. That is distinctly unfair, and I trust that as the right hon. gentleman grows older he will outgrow that tendency.
Let me say a word or two regarding the stand I take on trade, in order to make my position clear once and for all. I do not oppose trade; neither do I ardently worship it. As long as the circumstances persist which at present obtain, we Canadians simply must trade; first, to rid ourselves of our surpluses; second, to obtain those commodities which we need and which we cannot produce, such as citrus fiuits and the like; third, to enable us to have seasonal exchanges, so that in the winter time, for example, we may enjoy carrots, green vegetables and the like, which can be produced readily in warmer climates. At the same time we have interest to pay on debts. That interest can be paid only in goods and the goods can be exported only by trade. Again, we have life insurance policies in companies located in the United States and elsewhere. Upon those policies we must pay regular premiums which must be paid in goods, and goods can be exported only through trade. Then we have a great deal of raw material to distribute.
At the present time we are endeavouring to distribute the world's raw material by trade, and in so doing we are attempting an utter impossibility. Let no man forget that. We
are attempting also to place adequate purchasing power in the hands of our people by means of trade. In so doing we are again attempting an utter impossibility. These last two objects cannot be attained, and until those who are leading this country and the people generally throughout Canada clearly comprehend these latter two facts which I have laid down, we shall go on blundering, trusting to trade to do those things which trade cannot do.
Much has been made by the Prime Minister of the contention that this treaty is tending towards peace. During the time at my disposal I propose to discuss that aspect of the treaty, neither opposing the trade treaty nor defending it- as an economic measure, but treating it purely as a political measure in a world where war abounds. Our people in Canada want peace. A democratic government should give them peace. If this government cannot give them peace, at least it ought to follow those policies which are designed to lead to peace. I contend that this government in signing this treaty is taking a step which is not tending towards peace. Can the treaty help to prevent war? Absolutely not. When the Prime Minister maintains that it will do so, he is deceiving himself and all those who trust him.
In a Canadian Press dispatch reporting a speech delivered by Sir Samuel Hoare on February 10, 1939, I find a most interesting statement, in these words:
How often have I thought . . . when I was foreign secretary, that we tended in the years after the great w-ar to ignore the root of the causes of future wars.
Does Sir Samuel Hoare know? During those years Great Britain was striving for trade treaties. Does he think for one moment that in so doing she was removing the root causes of war? Manifestly he does not. He goes on to say:
Our first duty is to be ready to remove the causes of war.	[DOT]
To those words I say amen.
What are the causes of war? There are two main causes to-day. The first is the deficiency of purchasing power in the hands of the people within any given country of the world. The more we know about realities, the less we shall treat that statement with disdain. It was that condition which brought into power Hitler and Mussolini, and it is that condition which will bring into being a Hitler or a Mussolini in Canada unless it is changed. The second main cause of war is that in this world there are plenty of resources, but they are in the- hands of relatively few nations. The other nations are unable to get those
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

resources, or the products of those resources, by any means known to man, except by fighting. If we are going to remove the causes of war we must remove those two causes. For example, sir, in Alberta we have vast resources of coal. Italy needs coal, which she must import every year in order to keep her people from freezing. Up to the present time and under the present system we know of no way to enable Italy to get enough of the products of Alberta's coal fields except by . conquering and possessing Alberta. We want to remove the cause of war; seek it in this inability and remove it. I maintain that this treaty, or a thousand treaties like it, cannot remove that cause.
What is the cause of war? Is it lack of goods in this world? Let us see. I have in my possession a statement by F. E. Lathe of the national research council of Canada. On June 27, 1938, in Ottawa, speaking before the American Association for the Advancement of Science, that authority declared that mankind to-day can produce four times as much food as all the people alive can use. In the same speech he said there is a sufficiency of every other necessity in the world to give everyone an adequate standard of living. There is no lack of plenty in this world. The trouble is that we have not yet learned how to distribute it.
During the same convention another eminent authority spoke; this time Doctor Harold C. Urey, Columbia's Nobelist in chemistry. Before the convention he used these words:
There is little doubt but that much of the unrest of the civilized world for the past twenty-five years resulting in revolutions, new systems of government and world wide depression are all-
Note these words-
-rather closely related to this productive capacity, largely brought about by science.
Mr. Speaker, through you may I call the attention of hon. members to the fact that this is a revolutionary statement. It is a
statement of what seems palpably impossible -that we are fighting, having depressions, having upheavals, because of our large production. Yet those are the words used. And he goes on to say that profound modifications of our social and economic institutions must result from the clearly increasing productive capacity for material things that chemistry and other sciences make possible. There can be no doubt of the meaning of that man. I maintain that statement bears out my contention. We must leam to distribute. Lack of distribution within the country and among the different nations is the fundamental cause of war and troubles.
What is the cause of war? It is the unequal distribution of resources. I shall have to turn over to Hansard a chart which I wish all hon. members to see. This is a striking chart used by F. E. Lathe in his speech. I shall have to tell-

regret to interrupt the hon. member for Lethbridge, but I would ask him to confine his remarks to the trade treaty between Canada and the United States.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I do not see how in
the world a person can more closely confine his remarks to the treaty than by discussing the question whether or not it will tend to create peace, especially when the Prime Minister made that as one of his greatest arguments in favour of the treaty. The question of peace is the matter I am discussing. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I have laid down the statement that there is an inequality in the distribution of resources throughout the world, and that this is one of the causes of war. Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
Is it not clear why Germany, Italy and Japan must struggle with the nations which have those commodities in abundance, in order that they may be able to get their share? There is an inequality of distribution of this world's resources. This generation must discover a means whereby we can enable those three nations to get their full share of the production of those resources, without owning them, or they will arise every twenty or twenty-five years, when they are strong enough, and endeavour to seize them by force.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has declared twice in the house that in the present treaty Italy, Germany and Japan hardly profit at all-and we are supposed to be signing this treaty to get peace! Yet those three nations with whom we want to have peace are entirely ignored, so far as the benefits to be derived from the treaty are concerned.
How can this treaty help towards peace? I will grant it helps the United States, Canada and Great Britain. But Great Britain and the United States are not the sources of our potential danger, as the leader of the opposition has so well pointed out on two occasions before the house.
What is the cause of war? What does Herr Hitler say? Perhaps I may be excused for quoting a few salient passages from a recent speech he made. He may not be representing himself truthfully, but this is what he says:
In Germany 135 persons live on one square kilometre-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Order. Would the hon. member state the newspaper from which he is reading?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It is an Associated
Press dispatch from Berlin under date of January 30, appearing in the Ottawa Citizen. May I just quote again:
Where lies the cause of all our economic difficulties? (says Hitler). In over-population of our living space.
In Germany 135 persons live on one square kilometre (-358 square mile) without outside assistance and without the resources of former times.
"No people have been born to be "have-nots," and no people to be "haves." The conditions of possession on this earth have resulted from historical development."
And again:
Every people has the right to make its existence secure on this earth.
And again:
It has exactly the same right to participate in the exploitation of this world as any other people.
And again:
As things are, we must replace what we lack in material means by extreme industry and the greatest possible concentration of our labour power.
And again:
He for whom nature lets bananas grow into the mouth-
And, sir, if he was not thinking of the United States, and Canada and other parts of the British empire I ask you what was he thinking about; for if there is any people in the world born with bananas growing into their mouths-

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
"Yes, we have no
bananas."

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
We are those people.
-by themselves naturally has an easier fight for existence than the German farmer %vho must work hard all the year to keep his soil in condition.
The whole speech is replete with statements like that, which are pathetic. If we are ever going to get ourselves to the point where there is an understanding between us and the other great races of this world, we must commence now, and not delude ourselves into thinking that the signing of such treaties as this is the beginning of that understanding.
Do such treaties make the "have" nations help the "have-nots"? is the question to ask. This is a treaty among three "have" nations, the three greatest "have" nations in the world. By what conceivable means can it help the "have-nots," when the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon specifically stated that the "have-nots" were not to derive benefit from these treaties, except only incidentally?
May I now read statements of some men whose word ought to bear some weight with hon. members, regarding treaties somewhat similar to this one? I choose first the words of Sir Archibald Sinclair, Liberal leader in England. He is speaking about the Ottawa agreements. But before reading this, may I say that when the Ottawa agreements were signed I hailed them as a great achievement. That was because at that time I did not understand. To-day, without any reflection whatever on the good men who negotiated those agreements, men who in my judgment believed they were doing what was in the best interests of this country, I would certainly not praise those agreements. I agree with this man. Here are his words:
It was not until then-[DOT]
That is when the Ottawa agreements were signed.
-that the German people abandoned themselves to the frenzy of despair which we call

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
Hitlerism, and the tariffs and quotas of Ottawa, the economic armaments of the British empire, began to breed in other countries tanks, aeroplanes and warships, the military armaments of nation* which were determined not to go oil paying tribute to Britain but to acquire territories and raw materials for themselves in Abyssinia, in Spain, in China, in Austria, in Czechoslovakia, and perhaps ultimately in the British empire itself.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: What is the date of that?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
According to the record I have, this was delivered on May 11, 1938. At any rate it was near that time.
That is what one great authority says-I assume he is an authority; I hope he is not just talking political ballyhoo. He ought to be an authority. Those words are worthy of our respect. The Ottawa agreements were somewhat similar to the agreement that we are now discussing. They were a set of agreements designed to enable members of the select few who have been blessed by Almighty God with the good things of this world to keep these things unto themselves and away from the others.
I have another quotation of the same tenor. This is from Peaceful Change published by the Foreign Policy Association:
Through the Ottawa agreements of 1932, the members of the British empire, including India, the dominions and a number of British colonies, established a system of trade preferences, favouring each other, and discriminating against outside countries. Since the trade of the British empire amounted to 29 T per cent of the world total in 1934, such a policy is of serious concern to the rest of the world. Outside countries like Germany and Japan are thus placed at a disadvantage in all these imperial markets.
The trade treaty under discussion is an expression of a sort of Anglo-Saxon economic imperialism. Canada and the United States could manage to live largely without engaging in hot, successful commercial rivalry. That statement, without amplification, must seem strange, I know, but I could support it at great length. Canada and the United States, being blessed by providence with an abundance of all sorts of resources of every kind, are in a position largely to live without obtruding their goods upon the world markets and competing with the other nations who have to trade their goods on world markets in order to live. We do not need to extrude our goods in order to live; we are doing it merely as a means to distribute purchasing power among our people, simply because we have not yet learned a better way of doing it. Is it not hot, successful com-
mercial rivalry which tends to war? May I read some words of President Wilson, that great ambassador of peace:
Is there a man or woman, nay, is there a child in this audience, who does not know that the seeds of war are sown in hot, successful, commercial rivalry?
This treaty as far as Germany, Italy and Japan are concerned is tending towards hot, successful, commercial rivalry against them. Thus it does not tend to remove the causes of war; it tends rather to provoke war. I am not condemning the treaty; I am not saying that at the present stage of our progress it is not necessary for us to have such a treaty. But I am saying that any informed person who deludes himself into thinking that a treaty like this tends towards international peace is either culpably ignorant or culpably lacking in understanding. I intend to support the treaty, not because I am deluded into thinking it tends towards peace. It is a bargain economically profitable or unprofitable. But let no man trust to it for peace. If he does, he is leaning upon an aged and very much decayed reed which will break and let him fall.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I always listen with a great deal of interest to the leader of the social credit group in this house (Mr. Blackmore). I also read very attentively the statements he occasionally makes between sessions, and it is hard for me to reconcile the statement he made last fall immediately after the trade agreements had been signed between Canada, the United States and Great Britain, the treaties we are now discussing, with his attitude to-night, because in an interview he then gave to the press he stated that he was highly elated at the signing of the treaties. But this evening, listening to him, the only conclusion I could draw was that he was strenuously opposed to this trade agreement between Canada and the United States.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he not recall that I said in the course of my remarks upon this treaty to-night that as far as I could see it was in the interests of Alberta and in the interests of my constituency directly? I think he will grant that I said that.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The hon. member may have said that, but any one reading his speech in Hansard would be left with the impression that he was absolutely opposed to
the treaty.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Will he not grant that I stated repeatedly to-night that I favoured the treaty for economic reasons?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Anyone who will analyze his speech would say that it was seventy per cent against the treaty, perhaps five per cent for it, and nobody knows what the other twenty-five per cent was about, but I want to believe what he has just said. He mentioned that the people, the consumers, should be considered. But, Mr. Speaker, we are all consumers, and as consumers we have a right to expect that tariff changes will operate to our benefit. There is one thing that the Canadian people have come to realize perfectly during the last'four years of the present administration, and that is that tariff changes which have been made have been continually downward, not upward, and that for the consumers of Canada the cost of living has, by such action, been steadily decreasing, and will continue to do so as long as we adhere to that policy.
The hon. member also mentioned the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the House of Commons. I believe, that every member of the house and everyone who has seen how the Prime Minister has, for a great number of years, carried out his functions, realizes how patient he is with every section of the house, and with every member, in all matters pertaining to the parliament of Canada. I say that without fear of contradiction.
The leader of the Social Credit group spoke repeatedly to-night of the unlimited resources we have in this country, but I think we should be very careful about making statements of that kind. He mentioned that Italy, which lacks coal, could easily get coal from Alberta. Would he tell the house how feasible he thinks it would be for Italy to buy Alberta coal? A few years ago there was a bonus paid on coal by the federal government. In our section of the country, in northern Ontario, we have long and severe winters and we use a great deal of coal. We tried as earnestly as we could to use Alberta coal, but we could not use it economically for either domestic or industrial purposes. The distances were too great for economical transportation.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It is the hardest coal in this country.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: But it is not at all easy of access. The hon. member will not state that it is easy to bring Alberta coal to northern Ontario.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I said that we have the
hardest coal in this country in Alberta, forty-two miles south of Calgary.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Yes, you have coal,
wheat and cattle, et cetera

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The hardest coal in Canada, less than one-half of one per cent moisture.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: -but you lack many other commodities. It is no use saying that we have unlimited resources. We have limited resources, and they are hard to develop. I have mentioned northern Ontario. At the present time lumbering operations in my section of the country are conducted in a temperature ranging from fifteen to forty below zero for months at a time, and there is now nearly five feet of snow in the bush. Will the hon. member say that our natural resources are easy to develop? They certainly are not. Our mining is all done in hard, solid rock. Tins is a hard country; we have to fight every inch of the way, and if we have done so well among the trading nations of the world, this has been on account of the fine character of our population, its industry, enterprise and determination, which is the greatest asset any nation can have. Apparently the hon. member believes much more in the utterances of totalitarian leaders in Germany or Italy or some other countries of Europe than he does in his own government.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: How does the hon. gentleman arrive at that conclusion?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
When he spoke of the
nations that have not, he apparently did not realize that our markets are opened to Germany and Italy. Personally I have received a number of letters criticizing the action of the government because Germany and Japan receive most favoured nation treatment with respect to the commodities dealt with in this treaty.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: He quoted a press dispatch.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
There is no necessity
for Germany to fight for any raw materials she wants. She can get them if she wants them, like all other nations. Will the hon. member maintain that it costs Great Britain less than Germany or Italy to get the raw materials to keep her industries going? Germany and Italy have access to world markets the same as any other nation.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
But they have not the
credit.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It is their intensive
nationalism that prevents them from taking
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

advantage of that access. They do not want to trade with other nations of the world, and we have accordingly seen revolutions take place in the last few years. Mr. Cordell Hull, of the United States, only a few years ago, in 1934, stated that while the United States had made big mistakes on the tariff question and they have been changing drastically their policy in that regard in the last few years:
Extreme nationalism, if persisted in, is destined soon to wreck our entire structure of western civilization. In entering upon the negotiation of trade agreements, we are willing frankly to admit that we have erred in the past, that w'e have now repented.
Just as we set the vicious example of erecting the trade barriers of high tariffs which induced others to follow us, so now W'e are asking other nations to join us in an attempt to undo the damage our collective action has worked.
Surely the members of the social credit group realize that situation. It was not for reasons of trade alone that Germany annexed Austria. It was not for trade alone that she annexed the Sudeten from Czechoslovakia. Hon. gentlemen opposite should be fair and not "make statements which cannot stand the light of day, and in discussing a matter of this kind they should not attribute to the government motives which the government do not have. We believe trade treaties between the haves and the have-nots, treaties between all the nations of the world, -would foster the bringing about of universal peace, and it is the only way in which we can have universal peace.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Why not include the other nations too?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
They are included, at
the present time, many of them, and all of them that wish to come in. All that a country has to do is to show its willingness to trade with Canada, the United States and Great Britain. Only a few days ago a British statesman, speaking in the House of Commons at Westminster, I believe, said that it would not be necessary for Germany to get back her colonies to get raw materials because the raw materials of the British empire were always easy of access to Germany and Italy at the same prices as to other nations.
I am absolutely in favour of more and more trade agreements of this kind. When one looks at Canadian history over the past seventy-five years, with its succession of reciprocity defeats and revivals, it would almost seem that some force stronger than politics, perhaps some national selfishness,

kept alive the idea that Canada and the United States should not engage with each other in profitable trade, but we are gradually coming to a better understanding on that question. The echoes of previous general elections in this country come back to my ears. In 1911, for instance, we had that fine motto from the Conservative party, "No truck or trade with the Yankees," and only last fall they were talking of Canada's annexation to the United States as a result of the present trade agreements. A man who is presently a member of the upper house, and a minister in the previous government, made the statement that the signing of these trade agreements was one of the surest steps towards the annexation of Canada to the United States. He was trying to revive the old cry of annexation to the United States.
I was pleased to hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) say this afternoon that we should be ready to trade with other nations on a fair basis. How far away this is from the policy of 1930, when the then leader of the Conservative party was going to blast his way into the world's markets. His powder must have been very wet, because he was not able to do any blasting that I know of. The present leader of the Conservative party mentioned, I think, that the Hon. Oliver Stanley said that some of the features of the present trade agreement were "eyewash." Well, I remember what was said about the Ottawa agreements by one of the ministers of the British government; he said it was humbug, speaking of some of the actions of the then Prime Minister of this country in 1932.
The hon. member also said that the tariff protects labour and industry. I still have to be shown when a tariff has really protected Canadian labour. As to protecting Canadian industry, I am absolutely open-minded on that score. There may have been stages in the life of some of our industries at which they needed some tariff protection, but no one will deny the statement that in very many instances protection has been used to fleece the Canadian people who have been compelled to pay high prices by industries which have hidden behind the tariff wall.
The leader of the opposition appears to have lost some of his red-blooded Cana-dianism when he says that we cannot do very much, we 11,000,000 people, for the peace of the world. Surely a nation which is fifth in the world as far as trade is concerned should have its voice heard and respected in the concert of nations, where it should be heard on behalf of peace and harmony. This

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
agreement is one great step forward, showing not only that democracies can unite for the good of all, but that commercially speaking it is possible for nations to ally themselves for peaceful purposes. We have done a great deal for peace, and Canada should not take a back seat whether in the League of Nations or in the matter of trade agreements; for we are worldng nationally and internationally for the peace of the world, and appeasement between nations.
I believe the leader of the opposition was hardly fair to himself when he said this afternoon that we must have peace in our midst before we talk of universal peace. Surely he never meant that statement to be taken literally, because we have peace in this country, although there is some unemployment and some poverty to be dealt with, sometimes acerb discussions; but we are not suffering more than any other nation, and our condition in that respect is not any reason why we should avoid trying to the utmost by trade agreements and all kinds of activities to keep in the forefront ideas of international appeasement and the preservation of peace.
The leader of the opposition also expressed the opinion that Americans are much better traders than we are. Well, I have been quite a student of Great Britain, and I believe it would be difficult to drive a hard bargain against Britain. Old John Bull and Jack Canuck have the reputation of being good traders. We must always visualize this as practically a triangular trade agreement; it was made possible to some extent by the good offices and the willingness exerted not only by Canada but also by the United States and the United Kingdom.
As far as my own section of the country is concerned, we should be free traders in the full sense of the word, for the very good reason that we are primary producers. For every pound of our production we must of necessity find an outside market, and I maintain that the best markets we have are those of the United States and Great Britain. Some hon. memjpers seem to deplore the fact that we are so close to the United States. Cannot they realize what Australia, for instance, would give to be in as close proximity to the United States as we are? After all, in a good many instances we are running on parallel lines in our culture, civilization and way of thinking; our production is almost identical so far as our industries are concerned; our financial and industrial activities operate on much the same footing; and we are in the happy situation not only of having an 71492-69
American outlook but of working within the-orbit of Great Britain, within the commonwealth of nations, and acting as a liaison officer between Great Britain and the United' States, as well as enjoying those two fine markets which we so greatly need.
I desire to say a few words about the seasonal tariff on fruits and vegetables. I want the Ontario and Quebec producers of these products to have a full measure of protection so long as it does not interfere with the cost of living of the pioneers in districts like northern Ontario and northern Quebec. I know of many instances where the change in the seasonal tariffs has been the cue to certain dealers to over-charge the. people in-, our section of the country. I am not a free trader, and I believe that central Canada should enjoy a reasonable amount of tariff protection. Do hon. members know that in our section at the present time there is what we call a zone system? They may be surprised to know that when I am living in my home town I pay thirty-five cents a gallon for high test gas. In Ottawa you pay nineteen cents a gallon for the Same kind of gas. While those who live here are paying on their overdrafts on current accounts six per cent, we in northern Ontario have to pay eight per cent. That sort of thing applies all along the line. A premium has been applied against us as far as our section is concerned. If we criticize high tariffs it is because we believe we are paying exorbitant prices and helping other sections of the country to our detriment. All we want is fair treatment.
I was astonished to hear from the leader of the opposition and from the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), that in dealing with items of trade between Canada and the United States we should not include our exports of gold; that gold is not a commodity. Did the hon. members by that mean that, like King Midas of old, who had the power to turn into gold everything he touched, and who, in spite of all that wealth, starved to death, we must start and accumulate gold? As far as northern Ontario and Canada are concerned, when we have a surplus of that commodity we must dispose of it in outside markets. We have been fortunate in that respect because a few years ago the President of the United States found it possible to increase the price of gold to S35 an ounce. That decision has meant the lengthening of the average life of the old gold mines of northern Ontario and the opening up of new. ones, giving useful occupation to tens of thousands, yes, hundreds of thousands, of Canadian workers.

speechtext:
Speaking of this matter the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George answered thus, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) put this question to him, at page 477 of Hansard: "Is gold not a merchantable commodity?"
Mr. Cahan: No, gold is not a merchantable commodity in the sense that iron or steel or wheat is.
Well, I repeat that this shows how shortsighted some members of the opposition have been in their opposition to and their arguments against this trade agreement. Further, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said that we have exported to the United States 8258,367,247 in gold bullion, and that this should not be included in our export trade. Does he not realize that our producers of gold, and now the government, are always trying to get the best market possible? Do hon. members who speak on this problem realize that in 1933 the Conservative government stopped the selling of gold to anyone but the Canadian government? Do they think for one moment that any Canadian government, whether past or present, has not always done its utmost to find the best markets in the world for Canadian gold? I repeat that with the surplus of production of this commodity we cannot.keep it in this country any more than we can keep our excess supply of pulpwood or of sulphite or of grain. Will the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George say that we should send that gold to Germany, for instance? What price would Germany or Russia or the Scandinavian countries give for that gold? These are questions that must be very carefully considered when we are dealing with one of the largest wealth-

producing industries in Canada, which has greatly helped the nation during these times of stress. The hon. gentleman said:
But no trade agreement is necessary to induce foreign countries to accept bar gold. Gold is not an ordinary commercial commodity which is subject to customs duties, and gold has no place in trade statistics which are quoted to show the advantages of a reciprocal trade agreement between this country and the United States or between this country and any other country.
The same applies to all other production. We all know that in the past the United States government have used the tariff as an instrument for the protection of United States industrialists, and it did not always work for the prosperity of that nation. In my section of the country we must of necessity find outside markets; and the best market we have is in the United States. But the United States market is very sensitive. It is easy for that market to lose its equilibrium. I remember vividly two years ago before the increase in the cost of newsprint from $45 to $50 a ton, in my own constituency, in the whole of northern Ontario and northern Quebec, the newsprint and sulphite mills were working over-time shipping in some instances a whole trainload of newsprint in a day. But then the Americans began to buy more freely from the Scandinavian countries, and at the present time we have the sad spectacle of some of these mills running at only fifty per cent capacity, with the result that the prosperity which existed last year in that section is now gone. That makes a big difference to this country. We have no market in Great Britain for that commodity, nor have we in Germany or the other nations. Canada depends upon a freer interchange of commerce between this country and other nations of the world, because it must not be forgotten that we are on an export basis, and that freer interchange will prove beneficial to us in the long run. At the beginning of this session the leader of the opposition, speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, made an allusion to the present trade agreement. He had this to say:
There have been perhaps more or. less sub rosa, many complaints against this treaty, but the industries of the country may have been too frightened to express their opinions about it. Some of them appear to think it would be more or less unpatriotic to express an opinion against the treaty.
I never doubted the patriotism of our industrialists, our manufacturers, but I do know that when their interests are affected they are certainly outspoken and it does not take them very long to express themselves.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
If any one will take the trouble to read the various opinions which have been expressed by the industrialists of Canada with respect to the trade agreement, he will realize that that agreement has been wonderfully received by every business organization, by every industrialist in the country. Some of them refer to it as the 1939 model trade agreement, one that will be beneficial to Canada as a whole. Apparently the industrialists of Canada realize, just as those in the United States do, that at times it is necessary for them to make sacrifices. It is not necessary in this instance, and where it may seem that temporarily the trade agreement will not be satisfactory, a little reflection will suggest that in the long run it will prove beneficial to every section of our population. Many opinions have been quoted, from newspapers and various other sources, to show that the agreement should be acceptable to the dominion as a whole.
The opposition that was expressed in this house earlier in the session was more pronounced than it is at the present time. Nearly fourteen months ago, when the announcement was made by the government of a three-way agreement, the Conservative opposition thought they had something to work upon such as they had in 1911, and Mr. Bennett, when speaking in Halifax, tried to stir up the people. He told them that they must fight that agreement from the drop of the hat; that the trade agreements which the government contemplated meant that we were selling Canada's birthright. My hon. friends, however, sensing public opinion, realized that the people were in favour of the agreement; and in his speech this afternoon the leader of the opposition showed that he was fully conversant with the views of industrialists, farmers, primary producers and the Canadian people as a whole. He knows they are practically all in favour of this trade agreement between Canada and the United States, and that to oppose it would not be a popular move on his part.
Some people sometimes seem to believe that the government has no right to appeal to sentiment in support of agreements of this kind. Sometimes they are baffled by the attitude of the government. They always remain in the realm of hard facts, never considering what might be the outcome of any action taken. But I believe that this government should be sincerely commended for the work it has accomplished in the last four years, and particularly in this instance, in bringing together the two great Englishspeaking democracies. Canada has played a great role in that achievement. The leader
71492-69J
of the opposition said this afternoon that in' some parts of Great Britain the people were opposed to the trade agreement on the ground, that it called for too great a sacrifice. The economists of London and Great Britain, however, had this to say, that even the briefest study of the terms of the agreement, is enough to show how little could have been done without the readiness of Canada to offer her generous cooperation, and that Canadian and British business men generally should be gratified at the part the dominion has played in effecting the treaty.
So far as I am concerned, I do not wish to see any harm result from the treaty. I do not want to see any of our minor or major industries adversely affected. But- I believe that every Canadian industrialist after making a close scrutiny of the three-way agreement will realize that in the near future, if not immediately, the result will be beneficial to Canada. In our section of the country we are ready and willing to make any sacrifices that are necessary to the well-being of the country, and if in regard to vegetables and fruits we are paying fifty per cent more than the people in the older sections are called upon to pay, we are willing to make that sacrifice, but we do not want that to be used to the detriment of our people and for the purpose of providing profits.
It has been suggested that the textile industry will suffer from the present agreement. I have studied the situation carefully from that angle and have looked into the retail trade in my own locality. I have spoken with some industrialists and they do not believe that particular industry as a whole will suffer.
I do not believe that the present discussion will be as long or as strenuous as we at first ejected, for the simple reason that the Canadian people are an infallible political barometer. They have looked into the situation from all angles and have thoroughly analyzed it, and they realize that although the agreement may not be perfect in some respects, although in some instances it may have to be amended from time to time, the government through the agreement has been working for the welfare of the Canadian people.
It has done more, however. It has continued the policy of appeasement in the international situation. We see that it is possible for nations with diversified interests to come together in matters that are so important. Sometimes trade is the cause of war between nations. Trade may cause friction. But, unlike the leader of the opposition, I do not decry the fact that there has been over a century of peace between Canada and the United States.
I see no reason why we should not be proud

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
to mention that fact, and to reiterate it, because it is an evidence that the nations have found it to be to their mutual advantage to live peaceably side by side. It is a much happier sight to see the border between Canada and the United States practically unprotected; it is much better than if we had on the one side something like the Maginot line and on the other the Siegfried line. Our two nations live side by side, each benefiting and respecting the other, and I would never fear what one of the senators from the province of Quebec mentioned the other day, for example; that is, our annexation to the United States. It is possible for us to develop more fully within our own borders, and as we achieve a greater understanding of the mentality of the people with whom we are so closely affiliated we shall slowly but surely create a civilization of our own, on which our proximity to the United States will leave its imprint.
In my own name and that of the people whom I represent I want to express appreciation of the fine work that was accomplished by the Prime Minister of this country when, immediately after his return to power in 1935, he announced the negotiation of a trade agreement between Canada and the United States. Again last fall nearly all the citizens in my section were equally happy because! of the action taken by the government in again negotiating a trade agreement with that republic. As far as those people in my section are concerned, it will be absolutely impossible for any opposition effectively to criticize those agreements, which in my view represent great amity and understanding between the three nations involved, and present an example to all the world.
