speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1936, during the debate on the 1935 agreement, * I expressed the belief that there would be very few people in Canada who, of their own knowledge, could give a comprehensive opinion with regard to that agreement, because its implications were so wide that time alone would tell. If that was the case then, it is more than ever the case now. Not only have we the terms of this agreement, to use the Prime Minister's words of the day before yesterday, added to those of the 1935 agreement, we have also the other agreement, with which we are not primarily connected, between the United Kingdom and the United States. Then we have the further fact that the concessions we give under this agreement automatically go to thirty or forty other nations whose agreements contain the most favoured nation clause, and from whom we receive nothing in return.

In addition, there is also the provision for the [DOT] removal of the 3 per cent excise tax, the implications of which cannot be followed because of the complexity of the matter in its present position. Again time will tell.
This afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) used that exact phrase, that time would tell, and he believes that it is telling. As his reason for so believing he gave the January figures having to do with trade. I do not take that as a proper basis on which to measure the agreement, because last fall we heard from all quarters that various transactions were being held up waiting for January 1, when this agreement would come into force. So it will be interesting to see whether the imports and exports in February, March and subsequent months bear out the contention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In my opinion, however, the trade figures as between Canada and the United States over the last three years have told at least part of the story. A week or two ago the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) directed attention to the export and import figures between Canada and the United States. At that time the hon. member was dealing with what he considered a mistake which is now made, in including the export figures of gold. At the moment I am not interested in that feature, but it is quite evident that if you are going to compare export figures over the years that have passed you must compare comparable things, and if until 1935 the gold export figures were not included, certainly they must be deducted now.
I want to direct the attention of hon. members to the fact that for the calendar year 1935 Canada's exports to the United States amounted to $261,655,372. With the improvement in world trade in 1936 those figures rose to $333,916,949. Again in 1937 those figures showed a slight increase, to $360,012,143. Then, because Canada was feeling the reflection of the set-back in the United States, they fell off so that for the calendar year 1938 our exports amounted to $270,461,189. Now I want to look at the import figures. In the calendar year 1935, before the 1935 agreement had any effect, we bought from the United States $312,416,604 worth of goods. Those figures improved in 1936 to $369,141,513, and again they showed a notable improvement in 1937, to $490,504,978. Then, I assume for the same reason that our export figures fell, in 1938 they dropped to $424,754,993. In other words, in 1938 our export figures dropped back almost to those of 1935, but our imports remained $110,000,000 higher than those of 1935. So to that extent

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
it appears to me that the benefits which were derived from the 1935 agreement were benefits to the United States rather than to Canada; and to the extent that this SI 10.000,000 represented commodities which Canada could and did produce, to that extent we made employment in Canada so much more difficult.
There is another consideration to which I wish to allude because it is another thing that makes it so difficult to measure the implications of this agreement. I refer to the spirit in which commercial interests in the United States will carry out the terms of this agreement. I do not wish to be misunderstood ; I am casting no slur on the commercial integrity of another countiy, but I am drawing attention to the difficulty that our business men have encountered in the past in carrying out business transactions with that country. We know of so many cases of shipments, covering everything from silk dresses to tank loads of heavy chemicals, which have been sold and moved towards the border with the expectation that they would enter that country under a certain tariff item. They have been held up at the border; and when finally admitted, after incurring demurrage charges, after the business deal had been queered, the question was submitted to the tariff board of the United States and a ruling less favourable to Canada was delivered.
Two or three years ago a shipload of lumber left Vancouver for one of the Pacific coast ports. On arrival at that port the lumber cargo was refused. Eventually it was accepted under protest. Then that matter was carried through the courts in that country for two or three years, before the matter was finally adjusted. We had the famous instance only last fall of the regulation which was imposed, entailing the marking of every piece of lumber. Our lumber had been selling in the markets of the United States. It had come into competition with United States lumber. That competition was, to an extent, resented, and all sorts of methods were resorted to in order to make it more difficult for trade to be carried on in exporting from Canada under the terms of the 1935 agreement-to such an extent that eventually a regulation was passed making it necessary to mark every stick of lumber.
I know that regulation has now been removed under the terms of this agreement, through an arrangement whereby the agreement was arrived at. But the point I am making is, even if that particular method can no longer be adopted, can we really go ahead in the belief that the spirit of this agreement will be carried out in accordance with
our understanding of the spirit of commercial dealings? It is these things that make it almost impossible for anyone to give a general opinion as to the effects of this agreement.
On	all	occasions when trade	agreementscome	up	for discussion we	are	faced withthe charge that we do not wish to make trade agreements. On the other hand the view we hold, a view which was corroborated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the other day, is that the Liberal likes to make	an	agreement. And	we	are of theopinion that he likes making an agreement so much that he is ready to let it go through for a price which in our opinion Canada is not able to pay. We are perfectly ready and anxious to make agreements, but they must	be	agreements which	by	their termscommend themselves to us. The Liberal charges us with believing in economic nationalism. Well, if we believe in economic nationalism we have taken the most extraordinary way of showing it.	I say that
because in the case of the Ottawa agreements we succeeded in extending Canada's commerce, her buying and selling, far beyond the coasts of Canada, and we did increase trade with the countries of the commonwealth. The very making of those agreements resulted in the making of scores of trade agreements between the nations of the commonwealth and foreign countries. And there is no doubt whatsoever that the making of those agreements was a factor in inducing the United States to make trade agreements.
She of course had surrounded herself by a perfectly frightful tariff, a tariff passed by her congress, and one which could be altered only by congress. So long as that tariff stood, the United States could not make trade agreements. She never expected the Ottawa agreements to be the success they were, and she awoke with a shock to the fact that she' was no longer able to enter the United Kingdom market and make use of it for the removal of her surplus. She desired to get back into the United Kingdom market. If anyone wishes to talk about economic nationalism, I would ask this question: Is there a country in the world which has been a greater exponent of economic nationalism than the United States, with her successive increases in tariff. Tariffs were raised so high that she had surrounded herself with a barrier over which even she could not trade.
So, after two attempts, the President of the United States received power to make trade agreements with other countries. He was permitted to cut by 50 per cent the items in the Hawley-Smoot tariff. There were

Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement
certain other restrictions, but that is the main one. He was empowered in 1934 to reduce that tariff. Immediately the statistical officers of Canada and the United States proceeded to delve into the figures and facts of trade, and to lay the foundation for the setting up of an agreement between the two countries. A draft of that agreement was ready in the summer of 1935. But when it became apparent to the late administration that the concessions the United States expected Canada to give were concessions which in our opinion Canada should not give, the late administration declined to make the treaty. Of course, after the victory of the Liberals in the fall of 1935, the agreement was signed, and since then we have been testing the results.
Still the Liberals use the argument against ms that we do not wish to make agreements. But, Mr. Speaker, surely the difference between us is just this: The price Canada has to pay. That agreement was for three years. The period of three years has expired, and we now have a revision. It was put over with such paeans of praise that when its terms were announced the public read nothing but columns of eulogies in the press of the country. To such an extent did that obtain that the industries affected began to dig into the matter of the agreement to find out where the snag was that should need such a gas attack to put it over. And gradually industry has learned what this agreement means to them.
^ Just as it is not easy for me or any other individual member to take a general view of the whole picture and form an opinion, so there is an opportunity in the house for hon. members with particular knowledge of certain industries in certain parts of Canada to take part, in the debate and to give us the benefit of their wisdom.
I happen to have a little knowledge with respect to two industries in southern British Columbia with which the people I represent are very closely connected, namely the production of fruit and the production of vegetables. In the treatment of tariff matters in connection with fruit and vegetables the Liberal has ever been unfriendly. For some reason or another, which I have never been able to understand, the Liberal government has it in wrong for fruits and vegetables. I consider that this agreement is the third serious blow the Liberal government has given those two industries in the last ten years, and I am at a loss to understand why they should have done it.
Continually Liberals boast of the fact that a Liberal Minister of Finance created the dumping clause. What good was that, when they never used it? In 1926, when for a
IMr. Stirling.]
short time we held office, we put the dumping clause to work; for the first time the Canadian producer had the benefit of the Canadian domestic market during the period of his production, and I defy any hon. member to point to the harm which resulted to the consumer. The Liberals carried on that method of protecting the industry for two years. Then, in 1928, they wiped out all the values for duty, and the flood started again. The reason they took this action on that occasion was that the free trade section of the Liberal party, this party which the Prime Minister told us the other day was a unit in its actions, became so noisy in the councils of the government that the government removed those values for duty, and the markets of our producers were again wide open to the glut from the United States.
I think it is quite evident that the Liberal government realized that they had gone too far; for when the 1930 budget was prepared, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) introduced into it a new feature, for which some at least of the fruit and vegetable growers' associations had asked for a considerable time. There was the general tariff of 30 per cent on vegetables and 20 per cent on fruit, and, besides that, there was introduced item after item of minimum seasonal specific duties. The reason for that introduction was that towards the end of the production period in one of the states of the union, when it was extremely desirable to them to get rid of the surplus of their crop, looking across to Canada they saw there an excellent place to send it, unprotected as it was, and they were ready to dispose of it at prices which were next to nothing. It is obvious that 30 per cent of next to nothing is still nearer to nothing, and left alone it was no protection whatever. Hence this addition of minimum seasonal specific duties, below which the tariff could not drop. They were helpful as far as they went. But the Liberals would have nothing to do with the dumping clause.
When the Conservatives came into office again for five years, the values for duty were imposed, the seasonal tariff was maintained, and there was far better protection for the fruit and vegetable producers of all Canada than they had had before.
Then this government, that likes making treaties, made the 1935 one. They wiped out the seasonal duties and reduced the tariff to 15 per cent. True, they made use of the values for duty, although to a lesser extent, because they were dropped to 80 per cent of what they had been. I am quite ready to acknowledge the work of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) in carrying out

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
that policy; I have heard him say that he does not approve it in principle but that no better way of accomplishing the desired end had yet been attained. It is not an easy piece of work to decide the dates at which those values for duty should go into operation or be taken off, because the areas in Canada where these commodities are grown are pretty widespread and vary in their seasons. That was blow number two.
Now we have blow number three. In blow number three we have had the values for duty reduced again. They have been removed altogether from certain commodities; the period has been reduced, and the three per cent excise is gone. On top of all that we have had one-third cut off the preferences in the United Kingdom market. How the Minister of National Revenue could go to the Annapolis valley and tell the apple growers there that in his opinion the reduction in the preferences would not hurt them, that in his opinion the revised agreement would help the fruit industry, and that the cut in the preference was arrived at as a reasonable arrangement between the British, the United States, and the Canadian fruit grower, passes my understanding, because Nova Scotia with her export of barrelled apples to the United Kingdom benefited greatly by that preference. Before 1932 she met in those United Kingdom markets very large quantities of United States apples, the surplus of the United States grower, and but a small fraction of it, which the United States producer was ready to dispose of at bargain prices. And after the arrangement was made for the preference, there was a steadying of that United Kingdom market of which we in British Columbia, selling boxed apples, also had the benefit. It was a matter of great surprise to us that in the years following 1932 the United States growers were able to send into the United Kingdom market such very considerable quantities of boxed apples. But what did that mean? Our apples which are sold by the box are grown under exactly
the same conditions as in the states to the south of us. We know their taxes; we know their irrigation rates; we know their orchard costs; and all of these are similar to ours. We know their freight rates and brokerage. Breaking down the four shillings and six pence per hundredweight, which was our benefit in the United Kingdom market, into terms of boxes of apples, it amounted to forty-four cents a box. It was patent to us that without assistance of some sort the United States producer could not possibly be shipping in those quantities to the United Kingdom and taking forty-four cents a box less than we got. It was a great puzzle for some time how this was being done. But gradually it leaked out that the grower of apples in the Pacific states had been receiving federal assistance. It is not in the form of one definite subsidy paid, but apparently it reaches him under two or three different schemes that we know as the alphabetical schemes in the United States. But there it is; he is getting subsidy help. They made no bones about it last fall when these treaties were being discussed. Their growers talked to our growers; their papers referred to the fact that it did not very much matter to them what the two countries did with regard to this preference, they yet had tfie subsidy. The subsidy is referred to in the trade papers and the ordinary papers in the Pacific coast states, and there is no doubt that they are receiving federal help, whereas of course we do not. The only way, therefore, that the United States producer can benefit from this alteration, this giving up on our part of one-third of the preference, is that he will still further enlarge the quantity of apples sent into that market.
Hon. members who were here in 1932 will remember the care with which it was explained in this house that these preferences had been arrived at after detailed careful discussion between the United Kingdom, Canada and the other dominions. In this particular matter the other dominions, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, do not enter because their shipping season is different from ours. But here we are, three countries, the United Kingdom, Canada and the United States, all harvesting their apples at the same period of the year. Hitherto we have had the shelter of a preference, and by arrangements between Canada and the United Kingdom we have seen to it that various grades and sizes have been such as to conform with similar grades in the United Kingdom, so they have been quite favourably disposed towards the shipment of our apples

But now we are going to find in these auction markets a tendency for the United States grower to return once more to his dumping habits and to be ready to receive pittances for his surplus apples, which will set the price for us and for the United Kingdom.
It was commonly reported last year that the government, in approaching this matter, believed that only two constituencies in this country were affected, and it was stated- I do not know how true the gossip is-that they would be very sorry to lose the Minister of National Revenue.

And one other riding affected was one in British Columbia that they scarcely expected to win. But I would remind them that it is a much more serious matter than that. There are thirty-five ridings in Canada in which apples are grown commercially, and if we are prevented from making 'use of the export benefits of the United King'd0111 market, those apples which we cannot export will tend to back up on the Canadian domestic market, resulting in smaller prices: Every apple grower who sells commercially in Canada will feel the pinch; and if and when he feels the pinch, this government will also feel it.
I do not understand, as I said just now, why the Liberal government have again and again put this load on fruits and vegetables. There are other hon. members in a position to take up the story with regard to vegetables, and I shall have little to say about it; but it is a most important factor in southern British Columbia.
The Prime Minister tells us that the New Brunswick potato grower is pleased with the result of this agreement. My information is quite contrary to that, and I know that the potato producer and the potato industry in British Columbia are certainly not pleased with it; for whereas we let United States potatoes in free, there is no countervailing nature to that item. We have to pay; if we ever did succeed in shipping into the United States.
I would remind hon. members of this fact, which must always be borne in mind when we are dealing with these perishable products. Canada lies north of the United States. The United States from Texas up to Michigan is producing these successive waves of similar vegetables, and as they draw to the end of their season for whatever vegetable you are considering, they desire to get it off their domestic market so as to free that domestic market for the next vegetable coming along, and Canada is so handy as the dumping
XMr. Stirling.]
ground for these vegetables. It is therefore useless to point out to the fruit grower and the vegetable grower that the United States have made some small concession on certain varieties which we might be able to ship into the United States, because our northern country does not ship vegetables into a southern country.
The Prime Minister in his speech used these words in reference to this matter:
United States fresh fruits and vegetables are made available on easier terms to Canadian consumers in those seasons when domestic products are not on the market-
I have often stated in this house that I am not interested in what the tariff is outside the period of our production. He goes on:
-while the Canadian fruit and vegetable grower retains his domestic market in his own producing season.
I maintain that this is a totally inadequate statement after one has studied the terms of this agreement. I also maintain that during the years when tariff protection was given on fruits and vegetables, the consumer has not suffered because there has been ample competition within Canadian production to see to it that these perishable commodities should be sold, and not held for higher prices. But I would also remind the house that if the day comes when the Liberal government, continuing to deliver these blows at the fruit and vegetable industry, succeeds in either destroying this industry in Canada or so reducing it as to make it almost impotent, the consumer will suffer. Once you take away Canadian production and the Canadian domestic market, the result will be that the United States will no longer look upon Canada as a dumping ground but will have arrived at that vision which Mr. Taft saw in 1911 when he so greatly desired the market of the great Canadian northwest.
